speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), and again today the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), have asked or given notice of questions concerning the position of the Canada-United States bilateral air agreement. There has been some discussion of it in the house and outside the house, and in view of its importance I feel that perhaps a statement should be made at this time.
The bilateral air agreement entered into between Canada and the United States in June of 1949 is a continuation of the original air agreement, with some changes. Among the new features three United States air carriers were granted traffic rights at Gander on the north Atlantic route and have been exercising those traffic rights under temporary permit pending action on their applications for regular foreign carrier licences from the
air transport board. The applications of two of these carriers, Transworld Air Lines and American Overseas Air Lines, were approved by the board on December 1, and yesterday licences were signed accordingly. The application of the third carrier, Pan-American, has been approved in principle, and the licence will be signed on receipt of certain minor amendments which that carrier has indicated it is sending forward.
The United States government was also granted traffic rights at Edmonton on two routes, the first a transborder route from Montana, and the second a through route from the United States to the Orient. Applications have been received from Western Air Lines and from Northwest Air Lines respectively for licences for these routes. It is expected that these applications will be dealt with in the relatively near future.
On the Canadian side, in connection with the new routes granted to the Canadian government, the United States government has issued a permit to Canadian Pacific Air Lines for the exercise of traffic rights in Hawaii on its route to Australia. The Trans-Canada Air Lines application for traffic rights in Florida on its Caribbean route is now being heard by the United States authorities, and will, it is expected, be dealt with within the next few weeks.
On the third new route granted to Canada between Montreal and New York, Colonial Air Lines has opposed an application to the United States authorities for a permit and has succeeded in action in the United States courts which prevents the United States authorities from proceeding with a permit for Trans-Canada Air Lines.
That is what brought about the issue of the show-cause order which was given yesterday by the air transport board, and for which the hearing will be held on December 12. Colonial Air Lines will at that time be given full opportunity to indicate on what grounds it believes its permit from the air transport board for the service between Montreal and New York should be continued.
I should like to point out that this order of the board is one between the air transport board and Colonial Air Lines, related to the permit issued by the board. The actions or policy of the United States government are not involved, and the Canadian authorities are fully satisfied that the United States authorities have proceeded in good faith in

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 211, respecting the Department of Resources and Development.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CREATION OF NEW DEPARTMENT
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF STAFF FROM MINES AND RESOURCES OR RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one matter in relation to this bill which it may be difficult to deal with under a strict interpretation of the rules, because it involves a reference to another bill. I ask your indulgence, sir, that I may point out what appears
to me to be a limiting aspect of this measure, the purpose of which is to set up a Department of Resources and Development.
The bill defines the duties and powers of the minister, and the scope of the activities of the department. Sections 5 and 6 prescribe the broad application of the act. Section 5 relates to the development of forest resources, irrigation projects, national parks, the archaeology, ethnology and fauna and flora of Canada, as well as tourist information and services, housing and the trans-Canada highway. Section 6 provides that the minister shall have the control and management of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, and of crown lands.
There is a similar bill to create a Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. Already something has been said about the setting up of additional departments, and it was argued on the resolution stage that it is not desirable to increase departments simply for the purpose of finding a place for another minister. It is not sufficient to let the matter stand there, because if another department and another minister are needed for the business of Canada, then all members should certainly support a bill which is put forward for that purpose. I suggest that the creation of these two departments is likely to lead to a certain measure of inefficiency and wholly unnecessary duplication, as well as a loss of effort, which is the best possible reason for considering the advisability of the functions of the two departments being incorporated in the department which might then be properly called the Department of Resources and Development.
After all, mines, and technical surveys of our mining or other areas, definitely have to do with our resources, and most important resources. There is no sound reason for separating mining from the Department of Resources and Development, which is to have incorporated in its title the appropriate word "development", because many of the functions of the officials and civil servants attached to the two departments must necessarily be carried out in the same area and be based upon the same type of knowledge. Officials and civil servants who are called upon to go into the Northwest Territories, into the northern areas of Canada from one end of the country to the other, or into the forest and lake areas where mines are found and where technical surveys will be carried out, will be covering precisely the same ground. I submit that the creation of these two departments, instead of being a move toward efficiency, is a definite move towards duplication and is a waste of effort.

Resources and Development
My comments would not have the same validity if the government were charged with the responsibility for the development of resources; but it is not. It has a broad supervisory relationship to all resources, whether they be mines, forests or anything else. Under our constitution as it stands today, and as I believe it will continue to stand, the development of resources is exclusively a provincial responsibility. Over the years most important work from a technical point of view has been done in connection with mining, forestry and other resources by federal government officials, and it has been of great assistance to the provincial departments in carrying out their responsibilities. There is every reason why a province charged with the responsibility of developing mines needs a department dealing exclusively with that activity, because they need field men, men with highly skilled background, who are able to assist in the development of the mines of their own areas.
In the case of forests the provinces, having exclusive responsibility for the actual development thereof, must have separate departments to deal with an undertaking so large in scope. Over the years they have built up highly skilled staffs which deal efficiently with these problems. One of the things we should be on guard against is the setting up of departments which bit by bit, human nature being what it is, will seek to acquire responsibilities which only create unnecessary duplication, not only between provincial and dominion departments, but also between departments of the dominion government itself.
I submit there is not a single activity in the two bills setting up the Department of Resources and Development and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys which could not be handled much more efficiently by one minister, who could make full use of his staff so that trained men going down the Mackenzie, to the Hudson bay area, Ungava or any other part of the Canadian northland, would be able to carry out the duties that involve co-operation with provincial authorities without the necessity of another man being sent back to cover precisely the same ground hundreds and in some cases thousands of miles from the office in Ottawa.
Let us see exactly what the function of the dominion government is as to mines. So far as the dominion government is concerned, the most important thing is what it does not do, rather than what it does. It is infinitely more important that the dominion government avoid any limitation of mining development by unbalanced or excessive taxation which has no regard for the fact that mineral

resources are a wasting asset. It is much more important that there be no restrictions on the free market for mineral products, that there be no control which limits this highly speculative and challenging type of development, than it is to set up a new group of officials who will find new reasons for making it more difficult to carry out this adventurous but extremely important task. The duties properly related to the department of mines are such that they can be successfully carried out by a minister who is dealing with the whole broad picture of resources in Canada.
Surely we must look at this matter from the practical point of view. A minister is charged with responsibility; he has a deputy minister, his officials, his technical staff, and other employees. A minister of resources has before him a map showing all the rich resources of this vast country. How much better it is that one minister examine that map, so that if he is sending a group of individuals to some distant point, another minister in another department, who is looking at another map showing our resources, will not be sending another group to examine the same problems in the same area.
Every hon. member here will recall the broad outline of the report of that great statesman in the United States, Mr. Herbert Hoover, when he examined the governmental structure in the United States. Significantly enough, he was a well-known Republican and was appointed by a Democratic president to carry out this survey, because of his wide experience in the administrative problems of government. This commission under Mr. Hoover found almost incredible duplications of service. His report is filled with the record of officials going out to do similar jobs in the same areas. It indicated the possibility of saving, not millions but billions, in the over-all administration of the United States government. We have before us the kind of thing in respect to which a commission, or a committee of this house, examining the administration a year or five years from now, would say:	These two
departments never should have been separated. Any commission examining this from the point of view of administrative efficiency and simplicity would say that the department has not jurisdiction over the actual development of the resources. It has the responsibility of bringing together the federal government and the provinces in joint efforts in their common fields of interest. For example, in the case of highways, it has the responsibility of passing enabling legislation under which broad agreements can be reached in respect to activities that cross provincial boundaries. It would be said also that there was a measure

dealing with forest resources, under which the provinces could be brought together to co-operate in research, in forest protection, and in fire prevention.
I feel sure that any commission examining the structure of government a year or ten years from now would say that this is wrong from the point of view of administrative efficiency. I am not going to move an amendment, because the government must assume the responsibility for the definition of the administrative tasks that are to be performed. Unless the Prime Minister is convinced that the contention is sound, and that he should act upon it, no amendment will produce any further result than the argument that is put forward. This is not a case in which an amendment should be proposed simply for the purpose of having the views of the members recorded, which is the usual purpose of an amendment when it is recognized that it cannot be sustained.
In all earnestness, I urge that these bills be allowed to stand. The bill now before us should be amended by incorporating in it the powers included in the act respecting the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The addition of one or two sections to this bill will give to this proposed new department the wide supervision of all resources that the name, mines and technical surveys, includes. We would then have one businesslike, efficient department under a minister who could have charge of the resources of this country; and, with the imagination of a man with feeling for Canada, he would be able to make the most effective use of the civil servants working under him. If this is not done, let us all recognize the fact that the two departments will continue to increase in numbers and in the extent of their authority. From time to time groups of people from these two departments will be meeting at Aklavik or at the head of Hamilton inlet and one will say to the other: Well, boys, we did not know you were here; what a lucky chance that we have met! They will ask each other what they are doing, and they will find they are each doing precisely the same thing.
I urge upon the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, that he realize what any commission would do if it examined this measure. Let us deal with this now instead of at some later time.

speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the minister to the duties, powers, and functions provided for in this bill. It is the most important bill we have had before parliament for some time. So far
Resources and Development as the parliament of Canada is concerned, its jurisdiction is found in these various subsections to which reference has been made.
There is no doubt that in this country we have the greatest natural resources of any country in the world, and they are much coveted by others. The wealth of our forest resources is untold. Future generations will criticize this parliament if immediate steps are not taken to preserve the heritage we have in the forests. I agree with the suggestions my leader has made in this connection. It is linked up with the tourist trade. Many forest fires are caused by careless people. We should realize that these fires are destroying the by-products of wood and interfering with employment. The minister is right in utilizing paratroopers in fighting forest fires.
Speaking of irrigation and the development of water power, since I first entered this house I have always contended that Canada should have a national policy in this regard. We are one of the richest countries in the world in potential hydroelectric power. It is estimated that 45 million horsepower is available, and only about one-seventh of it has been developed, part of which is only seasonal. For many years we have been hearing about irrigation projects. I am sorry to say that little has been done in that regard, on either the prairies or in other parts of Canada. The development of irrigation is only in its infancy.
For many years I have suggested that there should be a national park in Ontario, linking up the crown property on the Ottawa river, the Rideau lakes, the St. Lawrence river, the Trent canal to the Severn river, around Muskoka, and the lake of Bays, the Parry Sound district and Georgian bay, up to the Maganatawan river, and through new Ontario to the head of the lakes. These are all properties held by the crown in the right of the dominion or the right of the province. There is no reason why Ontario should not get a share of these parks. At the moment there is a small park near the St. Lawrence, and another up on Pelee island; but there is really no national park in Ontario. This results in the loss of a great deal of the tourist trade. I believe the time has come when, without expense to the country, we could link up the crown properties I have suggested around the great lakes and inland waterways of the province of Ontario. A hotel system could be developed along with it, and Canada could be made something like Switzerland. There would be winter sports and all that sort of thing. It would mean a great deal of business, in winter and summer alike, to the people in this country.
2586	HOUSE OF
Resources and Development
Mention has been made of tourist information and services. We have received only a small part of the wealth which we should receive from a proper development of the tourist trade and kindred services. For a great many years this country has not received proper advertising along those lines.
In connection with housing, I am sorry there is no cheap land in Toronto. There used to be a Toronto district including Peel, Ontario, and York counties. Land was available at $6 per foot within the city limits, and now it is as high as $65 a foot. There is not even land available for people to build houses under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation schemes. There is no steam suburban service such as Montreal has. I shall not go into that in detail this morning, but it is not a luxury; it is an economic necessity. When you find there is only one train a day out of some of those places in York county, and without commutation service, then it is another matter. Western Ontario, and especially the Niagara district, is suffering untold loss owing to the choked and cramped railway facilities available. We seem to be spending a great deal of money on our United States affiliation of the Canadian National, but not within Canada.
I shall not refer to the trans-Canada highway bill this morning, but I believe it will have to be read in conjunction with this particular bill. The other morning I was glad to hear the minister say that as pioneers in the good roads movement the provinces and municipalities which have gone ahead with this work will be recompensed.
I commend to the house the general principle of this bill. We have a great asset in our natural resources, and with the duties, powers and functions the minister now has, we should be able to start to develop them.

I should like to say a few words with respect to the remarks made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). His objection to this bill is based upon what might be called the overlapping of departmental activities as between the federal and provincial governments. So far as my own section of the country is concerned, which is highly mineralized, the people are satisfied with the government policy implied in this bill. I believe the same thing can be said of the mine owners. There is no doubt that in a federated state one must look for some amount of overlapping. No one would say that because we have a minister of agriculture in each of the provinces, the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa should be abolished. The same thing applies to mining.


I do not believe the leader of the opposition would say that there has been overlapping between the central government and the province of Ontario so far as mining is concerned. There is no doubt that the national research bureau, as well as other departments of the government-

subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF STAFF FROM MINES AND RESOURCES OR RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but, to keep the record straight, I most emphatically state that there has been duplication.

subtopic: CREATION OF NEW DEPARTMENT

speechtext:
No doubt there has been, but that is something we must expect in a federated state. No one would say that because there is some duplication in a provincial department, the federal department should be abolished; that is the point I am making. I was going to say that even the department of mines in Toronto-and I know whereof I speak-has benefited from research that has been undertaken by the central government; and this applies to several other activities. The same applies to forestry. It is true that the Northwest Territories have not the forest resources that we have in Ontario, but there is no doubt that the department of forestry has developed information which is useful in all parts of Canada.
I know something about the necessity for setting up this department, and I can say that it is a step in the right direction. The mining interests in Canada are satisfied with the proposal that has been put forward. I have not the time to present the briefs and recommendations that have been placed before me during the last ten years, urging the federal government to establish a special department for mining on account of its great importance in our economy. The leader of the opposition stated the position correctly when he said there was a mutual interest in the federal and provincial aspects of mining.
A few years ago, when the Canadian dollar was brought to parity, there was an immediate request from the gold mine owners who were primarily interested. I received dozens of telegrams and telephone calls.stating that the action of the government would harm the production of gold in Canada, and that some remedial measures should be taken. The department of mining is a necessary department, and a proper one for the federal government to administer. In common with the leader of the opposition, I do not believe in extravagance. Surely we do not need a Hoover commission in Canada; our situation is not comparable with that which prevails in the United States. There may be some departments that are overstaffed, but, so far as I am aware, there are very few of them.
I believe there is a method of liaison among all these departments and the provincial

departments. For instance, there is the Department of Justice and the Department of the Secretary of State. They fulfil a purpose which has to do with the application of justice in Canada. But who will say there is overlapping in these departments?
I am voicing the sentiment of my section of Ontario when I say that I am entirely in agreement with the formation of the three new departments. Here and now I want to compliment this administration upon forming the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. They will have their hands full if they want to look after the northern part of our country and the mining interests of Canada as a whole. The activities which will be undertaken in the future by these new departments will undoubtedly prove to be of great benefit in the development of our natural resources on a national scale.

I beg the hon. member's pardon; I thought he had made the definite statement. There is vast timber wealth in the Liard, Mackenzie and Yukon river areas, timber limits that have never been surveyed or officially noted. Tremendous forest fires destroy much of that timber, and when one realizes that we have no department to look after those resources, one cannot help being concerned. It is true that we have civil servants whose work has to do with these matters, but we should have a department headed by a minister who would be responsible for this work. Think of all the gold and other metallic wealth which has been taken out of that part of Canada, the quantities of base metals that are known to exist-and many of these areas are mapped by the surveys and mapping bureau-and the great wealth of oil and petroleum at Norman Wells and elsewhere.
I have gone along the Mackenzie river and have seen the oil running out from the shores
Resources and Development into the stream. I have seen a gas well up beyond Norman Wells which has been burning since Alexander Mackenzie passed through there in 1793. All these vast resources should be utilized.
The leader of the opposition objects to the creation of a mines department. speechtext: I wish, Mr. Speaker, to correct a possible misapprehension. I was not suggesting any limitation of activities in regard to mining; on the contrary, I emphasized their importance. speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think any of us misunderstood the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). I think we all understood that he was anxious, as are all of us in this house, to adopt the most efficient methods to promote the use of the great natural resources with which our country has been so bountifully blessed. As I see it, the only difference of view in this respect was that the leader of the opposition felt that this work might be more efficiently done under one department than under two departments. I thank the leader of the opposition for his constructive suggestions, and I thank the other hon. members who have participated in the debate. I think it has been shown that we are all

Resources and Development anxious to do that which will ensure the most efficient job in providing for the development and use of these resources.
I can assure the leader of the opposition that the matter of having these activities provided for by the two bills, No. 211, dealing with resources and development, and No. 212, dealing with mines and technical surveys, was carefully considered, and it was felt that it would be desirable to have two ministers responsible for those activities. One of them, the Minister of Resources and Development, would be principally concerned with the works and undertakings in process, whether for the federal government or in collaboration with the provincial governments. Many undertakings will require close collaboration between the federal and provincial authorities in order to bring about that measure of development which will be of benefit to the country as a whole. It was felt that all matters having to do with the physical works required to promote that development should be under one department, and that this would be quite enough to engage all its time and attention. It was felt that there should be another department which would be more in the nature of a service department, one which would be concerned with the making of scientific investigations which provide the data used sometimes by provincial administrations but oftener by individuals or groups of individuals who make them the foundation of their enterprises. This is the division that has been attempted in these two bills. The objective has been, on the one hand, the promotion of the physical works required to bring the resources into use, and, on the other, the scientific investigation which is necessary as a preparation for development work. In considering these bills hon. members will find that this is the line of demarcation that has been drawn.
The assistance of the Department of Mines and Resources has been sought for a number of years by those who have interested themselves in this highly speculative activity, as the leader of the opposition has described it, the results of which, however, have been of tremendous benefit to the Canadian economy. There has been pressure for a long time to have a department that would be specially concerned with the preparation of the basic information and data upon which the mining industry could rely when engaging in this highly speculative activity. There is no desire or attempt to invade the provincial field. However, all hon. members know that the services provided by the federal government with respect to surveys, assays and analyses have been of tremendous value in
tMr. St. Laurent.]
channeling properly these speculative activities, the results of which are of such benefit to us all.
I gave the approximate figures of the staffs in these two departments-something of the order of 2,000 to 3,000 in each; and I am sure the ministers and deputy ministers who will be charged with the responsibility of those departments will have, not overlapping jobs but full-time jobs, and that it will be in the public interest to have one of them specially concerned with pressing forward the works undertaken and the other concerned with the gathering of information and scientific data that will induce others to proceed with additional works of development.
It is in the interests of the development of these resources and their being brought into use for the improvement of the living conditions of all of us that these activities should be prosecuted with the greatest possible vigour and intensity. I hope it will appear reasonable to hon. members that there should be these two departments, the one pushing ahead works already undertaken, and the other preparing the field for vast new undertakings.

Resources and Development
The Prime Minister has said that sometimes delay is the result of difficulty in obtaining printed documents from the king's printer.
I would remind him that this year we had an example of delay on the part of the king's printer that did not interfere with compliance with the law on the part of the minister concerned. I refer to the public accounts and the report of the Auditor General. The law provides that, if parliament is sitting, the report must be laid on the table on October 31. On October 31 the Minister of Finance rose in his place and said that he did not have a printed copy of the report, but would table a typewritten copy. The report was thus made public, the press had access to it, and the law was observed. As a matter of fact, some of us did not get our copies until a few weeks later, but that did not mean that the law had not been carefully complied with by the Minister of Finance.
As the Prime Minister is probably aware, there have been four or five cases this session in which delays have occurred, and in not one case did the minister or the parliamentary assistant, when laying the report on the table, indicate that there was delay, explain it, or apologize for it. For instance, the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year ended March 31, 1949, should have been tabled, according to section 7 of the Department of Trade and Commerce Act, on October 6; it was not tabled until November 23, seven weeks late. There was no explanation or apology.
Similarly the Canadian Maritime Commission Act provides that the report must be completed not later than June 30 and must be laid on the table within fifteen days after the opening of the next ensuing session of parliament. In other words, that report should have been tabled by September 30 of this year. It was not tabled until November 24, eight weeks late. Again nothing was said by way of apology or explanation. Something else having happened in this connection this year, which is very well known, it is natural that I should begin to wonder whether these requirements are being complied with; hence the discovery of the information I am now giving.
The reports of the auditors in connection with the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act-I mention these two acts together, because the auditing is done at the same time-should have been tabled by September 30, according to the provisions of those two acts. They were not tabled until October 11, eleven days late.

I have all of these sections before me, but I have not taken the time to read them. As I have said already, the Minister of Finance made it clear that the law could be complied with even when the king's printer has not produced the printed copy. I urge that more care should be taken to observe laws of this kind. The proposal which the Prime Minister has made as to uniform procedure should be acted upon. If a minister cannot keep the law, he should at least explain to the house what has happened, and I am sure that in such circumstances the house would be generous. Since we are making laws which we expect the people of Canada to observe, I think they should be observed by the government as well. Surely that is not asking too much.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that motion for third reading has been made, a procedure to which I do not think hon. members will object, I should like to exercise my right to make a few comments in regard to one matter that came up in the course of discussion. I wish most emphatically to go on record as saying that I believe it is only a question of time before someone examining these two departments will come back with a recommendation that they be one department.
I should like to deal with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette). I recognize that the hon. member is keenly interested in mining, as all of us are, whether we live in a mining constituency or not. The hon. member said he felt sure that if this was the United States, Mr. Herbert Hoover would be the first to suggest that there be a department of mines.
I think the hon. member left the impression that there is a department of mines in Washington. There is not, and Mr. Hoover did not recommend that. On the contrary his recommendations all involved simplification of departments. Mining activities are under the department of the interior at Washington. That department embraces most of the subjects covered by the two bills now before us. For instance, the Department of the Interior at Washington covers mining, the bureau of land management-which is all land-Indian affairs, geological surveys, land reclamation, park services, fish and wildlife, and a number of other details, including technical surveys and matters of the kind which are embraced in these two bills. There are additions, but I only wish to emphasize now, because I am certain the matter will come up for discussion

again, that those who desire the efficient development of our mines would certainly wish to have it done in a way that will bring the greatest possible information to the public.
We are not dealing directly now with a department of mines. We are dealing with a measure which I suggest could have been amended to include mining activities. If we had done so we would have followed the practice that is followed in Washington. When I say that, I do not mean that we should follow the pattern of Washington. I raise the question because of my belief that the inquiry conducted into the administrative structure of their government was a most important one. It was at that point that the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), who is keenly interested in the whole subject, suggested that they would not think of not having a department of mines at Washington. They have not a separate department of mines, and for the very good reason, in my opinion, that the whole subject should be embraced under one ministerial head, with different branches dealing with the various subjects related to the resources of the whole country.
I intend to say nothing more, other than that the vote on third reading will be on division. I have urged that there be an amendment to the bill, purely for the purpose of seeking to produce the most efficient results. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has put forward reasons, which appear sound to him, why there should be separate departments. I simply wished to indicate why I feel it would be better if it were not done in this way, and also that in the United States they do not follow the practice of having a separate department.

speechtext:
I want to deal briefly with this bill, without repeating the remarks I have already made as to the consolidation of the two departments.
It must be remembered that the mines department of the dominion government deals with the broad problems of mining and information related thereto; it is not responsible for the direct development of the resources except to the extent that such information may contribute to the desired result.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CREATION OF NEW DEPARTMENT
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF STAFF FROM MINES AND RESOURCES OR RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY
speechtext: Perhaps the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) would add that it deals with such mines as may be in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.

subtopic: CREATION OF NEW DEPARTMENT
subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF STAFF FROM MINES AND RESOURCES OR RECONSTRUCTION AND SUPPLY
speechtext:
Yes, such mines as are outside of existing provincial areas, and there are some increasingly important mines in that region. Having said that, I want to emphasize the fact that the department in Ottawa has been the source of extremely useful information which has been the basis of discoveries of the utmost importance. The most romantic and dramatic story of discovery of mines in Canada was that concerning the finding of the Eldorado mine on Great Bear lake. Many people have forgotten, if they were ever aware of the fact, that the records in Ottawa played an extremely important part in the discovery of that mine. This may well be remembered in setting up the organization under the new terms of authority.
When those who intended to seek minerals in that area were about to set out on their expedition, they came to Ottawa to find out what they could about records of mineral possibilities in the Northwest Territories. They examined the original records of Samuel Hearne, who had covered the area in the eighteenth century when he was going through the Northwest Territories in the Great Bear lake region and on to the Arctic. He described evidence of rich minerals he had seen on the face of jutting rocks on the shore of a lake which at that time had no name, and which in fact did not appear on any map of Canada in anything approaching its actual shape until the early thirties. It was only then that any map existed which showed the actual shape of Great Bear lake, one of the largest bodies of fresh water in Canada.

Mines and Technical Surveys From Hearne's description and the type of promontory outlined by him, they decided to look for the great promontory where he had recorded this rich outcrop so many years before. What was found was the very thing Hearne had discovered one hundred and seventy years earlier. The gossan that was seen from the aircraft led the prospectors to the very point that had been described, toward which they were first attracted by what they had seen ' in those early records available in Ottawa. From that discovery came not only a great and important mine, but also a substantial contribution toward the production of the atomic bomb in the last war. I mention this to re-emphasize the vast importance of detailed information. We have advanced a great distance from the time Hearne travelled those waters in a canoe to the point where another important mining area was discovered through the opportunity to examine air maps of northern Manitoba. The development of the rich mineral resources in the God's lake area came about through an examination of air maps of that district which showed promising indications of what have turned out to be very productive mines. There is an accumulation of information through the years that can be of immense importance in the development of those areas; and as surveys are carried out, as survey parties report their information, and as the various indications of mineral possibilities are brought back to Ottawa, I urge that all this information be indexed in the satisfactory way in which it has been done up to now, and also that something be done to encourage an interest in that information on the part of those who at some future time may find these resources a matter of practical interest.
I say this because I know that many people directly interested, in the discovery of mines have never had occasion to think of searching these records for suggestions which may be contained in the information there available. With the new scientific developments that tell us so much about what lies beneath the surface of the earth, these records are becoming more useful; and I urge that in addition to carrying forward this work at an ever-accelerated rate from the point of view of information, every practical step be taken to encourage, in the minds of young people in the mining technical schools and the engineering branches of our universities, an appreciation of the vast storehouse of knowledge that already has been accumulated here and will be accumulated in the years to come.

From end to end of the estimates, in public works and every other department of government, it is engineers, engineers, engineers. I am wondering to 45781-165
Mines and Technical Surveys what extent this Department of Mines and Technical Surveys will duplicate the work done in the provinces. Each province has a department of mines which has its engineers and geologists and is doing a practical job of work in connection with our resources. With all the engineers and geologists we have in the mines department in Ottawa, certainly we must be duplicating a great deal of the work done by the provinces. From the start I did not see that this was necessary. I believed it was necessary to unscramble the Department of Mines and Resources in order to find out what many of its branches were doing; but in my view the creation of another department, with another minister and a lot more engineers and so on, in order to duplicate a great deal of the work being carried on by the provinces, is quite unnecessary. This minister, whoever he may be, is going to have a pretty good job. I suggest to the Prime Minister that he should get this minister a whistle such as they have on peanut stands, so he can blow it occasionally and let us know he is around.
I have gone all through these estimates and had a look at the provisions for engineers and other technical men in our departments, and I think that handing over our resources to these people merely adds up to technocracy. I suppose, and hope, that the Department of Resources and Development will be presided over by an engineer, such as the present Minister of Reconstruction and Supply; and I think mines and technical surveys logically belong to that department. If that minister is to be in charge of the development of our resources he should have under his direction those working on the resources from a geological standpoint and otherwise. I cannot understand why they should be separated. My conception of this department always has been that it contains a group of experts who are pioneering, who are not duplicating the work done by the provinces but who have knowledge of our frontiers and are pushing them back, gathering information which the provincial departments are not gathering and making that information available to them. But I cannot visualize the department, as I have come to know it since I have been in Ottawa, carrying on that sort of work.
I agree with what was said by the leader of the opposition, in his emphatic way, that this department should come under the other one. It is unnecessary to create a new department. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose
of the bill is to set up a department which will be charged with citizenship, immigration and Indian affairs. The matter was discussed at the resolution stage. It was stated then, and I now repeat, that the object in all these activities is to make Canadian citizens of those who come here as immigrants, and to make Canadian citizens of as many as possible of the descendants of the original inhabitants of this country.
As hon. members are aware, the responsibility for immigration and Indian affairs was heretofore with the Department of Mines and Resources, and the activities with respect to citizenship were with the Department of the Secretary of State. During the war period and in the years immediately following, immigration into this country was quite restricted, and has been increasing from year to year. There is a probability that there will be an increasing number of persons admitted as immigrants into this country to share with us the advantages and responsibilities of developing the resources of Canada.
With respect to our residents of Indian descent, happily for the last several years there has been a change in the previous trend. That trend had been toward a diminution in numbers. This however has been reversed to a point where there is now an increase in the number of residents of Canada descended from the original inhabitants of this country. With the additional health services being provided for them, I believe that trend will become definite, and that we may look forward to a steady increase in the number of residents of Canada descended from the original inhabitants.
That being so I believe it would be the desire of all of us that everything possible be done to facilitate the development of a condition in which they might be expected to take their place in increasing numbers in our Canadian citizenship. All hon. members know of individual cases where descendants of the original residents have abandoned the protective provisions of the Indian Act and have become Canadian citizens. We know of the contribution they have made to Canadian national life.
I am sure it is the desire of all of us that everything within reason which can be done to further that movement should be realized. As hon. members know, there have been a great many requests for the setting up of a department which would deal with these human resources of the Canadian nation, and


the sole responsibility of which would be the proper development of those human resources.
That is the purpose for which the government is suggesting to the house the establishment of a separate department to assume that responsibility and to discharge the functions required to bring about as expeditiously as possible the integration into the citizenship of this nation of as many as possible of those who come here as immigrants and of those who had resided here and who are descended from the original residents.
It is for that purpose that the establishment of the department is suggested. Then, as to the government's policy with respect to immigration, I do not know that I could add very much to what was said by the former prime minister in his statement to the house on May 1, 1947, which is to be found at page 2644 and following of Hansard for that session, and the statement I made to the house on March 11, 1949, concerning the modifications that had been made to the regulations in connection with the admission of immigrants.
A large number have been admitted to this country in the last couple of years. There have been a considerable number of those unfortunate persons who were in displaced persons camps in continental Europe. I think that, generally, they have fitted themselves into Canadian life without very much embarrassment to any of our Canadian people. It is my view that our experience in that respect has demonstrated that, while it was principally on humanitarian grounds that these people were admitted to our country, they will ultimately prove that the bread we cast upon the waters is returning to us.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words in the debate on second reading of this measure. I am wondering if the reasons for many of these changes in the matter of setting up additional governmental departments are not similar to those which I expressed when the resolutions were before the house last Saturday. I know the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) are making strenuous efforts to establish a case for an extra minister of the crown, but I think it boils down to this, that the argument is for another minister more than it is for the necessity of an allocation of duties among the various departments. I should like to repeat what I said before. I think the government ought to have said to the house, "We want another cabinet minister and are taking this means to provide the extra portfolio." The arguments that have been offered have been

circuitous and in some cases not very sound in respect to the need for an extra portfolio such as is envisaged by this legislation.
I think most hon. members will admit that immigration has been a very important part of governmental work and I know many have felt that a deputy minister of immigration would perhaps be desirable and acceptable in view of the importance that branch has now assumed. At this point I should like to pay a tribute to the present director of immigration, Mr. Jolliffe, who has been identified with this branch for so many years and who in so many instances has exercised fairness and judgment and common sense in dealing with the problems of immigration. I think his attitude meets with the approval of most hon. members, regardless of what section of the house they occupy. Now that the new legislation is before us I do not think that I would object strenuously to the setting up of a really important department to deal with immigration with a proper deputy minister at its head.
However, this was not mv main reason for rising at this time. I think this shuffling of the ministry so far as the allocation of work is concerned is wholly unjustified at this time, particularly with respect to citizenship. While I am in certain agreement with the Prime Minister about citizenship and immigration going together, still I do not like the idea of this branch of government being separated from the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley). In saying what I intend to say I intend no reflection upon the Secretary of State, but the fact remains that in this shuffle the Secretary of State is having something taken away from his department when perhaps something should have been added. I would hope that this would be taken into consideration by the government in making any move.
The portfolio of the Secretary of State- there are some others I could name as well-does not entail the effort and labour that some of the other portfolios do. If we are going to have more portfolios, then I submit the government is in duty bound to consider whether the present allocation of work among the ministers of the crown is proper. I do not think it is, and I do not think parliament thinks it is. It would now appear that we are to have 22 ministers of the crown. Twenty-one would seem to be sufficient and perhaps might be considered too many. We have left the war and transitional periods behind and I fancy the public in general would like to see some retrenchment rather than expansion in the number of portfolios in the government.
Citizenship and Immigration
I should like to have the Prime Minister's assurance that this shuffling about will not mean an additional cabinet minister. I think that is something the public would like to know and I ask the Prime Minister to give us that assurance before the debate concludes To me it seems to be merely a matter of having the work and services properly allocated and distributed among the available ministers of the crown. While this objection may not apply to the other two instances with the force that it applies to the present instance, I think that should be considered. There is perhaps much that can be said in favour of having these two branches of the government combined in one department, but if it is going to mean another minister I think that could be avoided by a proper allocation of the duties having to do with citizenship and immigration. I think that with the present members of the cabinet the Prime Minister will find that the work will be in good hands.
I should like to impress upon the government the great desire that some of us on this side have to see to it that the cabinet is kept within bounds so far as numbers are concerned. No doubt a great many representations have been made to the Prime Minister with regard to men who it is felt ought to be in the cabinet, but I suggest that with his large following he should steel himself against the idea of adding to the number of cabinet ministers. A should like that to be taken into consideration because I think it is out of joint with the times to add another cabinet minister, at least until those who are holding portfolios in the government find that their duties are such that they are overworked and have no available time to handle these extra departments. I repeat, I should like to have the assurance of the Prime Minister at some stage that this will be done.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the necessity was with regard to the other two departments that have been created by the legislation that preceded this bill, but I feel it is not only appropriate but desirable that immigration and citizenship should be in one department. I am glad that there is a bill before us for that purpose. I always found it to be a rather curious situation when writing about matters of immigration that I had to write to the Minister of Mines and Resources. It did not seem to me it was a very appropriate situation. Furthermore, and again expressing no opinion as to the necessity for any new department, I believe the Minister of Mines and Resources had too many different kinds of departments under him. Citizenship and Immigration to follow the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) in the reasons he gave for creating this new department. The person who is free from temptation and pressure can indeed be strong, but whether or not he can take credit for that I do not know.

Mr. Speaker, I think all members of the house will be pleased with one particular feature of the bill. I refer to the fact that the Indian affairs branch is being given a somewhat larger place in the new department. I sincerely trust the new minister who is appointed to take charge of the department will give this great problem the attention which it merits. As the house knows, a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons was set up in 1945 to examine the Indian Act. As a member of that committee I think I can say with fairness that some excellent recommendations were made to the government in the final report of the committee, and also that a good many changes were suggested in the Indian Act which up to this time have not been implemented.
I am not going to be entirely critical of the delay that has been occasioned by the study of the proposed legislation by the Department of Justice. I realize it is a far-reaching measure, and that a great deal of study and thought must be given to it. Nevertheless I sincerely trust that when the new minister takes charge of the new department he will take aggressive steps to see that the bill is taken out of the hands of the Department of Justice and brought forward to the House of Commons. I hope the next session of the house will see the revised Indian Act introduced.

Mr. Speaker, there is one feature of the bill which I should like to mention. I think the provision as to immigration is one which should be given careful examination when the department is being organized because we either have a policy in regard to immigration or we have not. If we have a definite policy it should be clearly understood, and the activities of the department should be carried on in relation to whatever the stated policy is. One of the greatest problems that face those who seek to come to this country through the immigration agencies now in operation is the difficulty of obtaining the various requirements to come here without a measure of assistance that is
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
usually not available. If we are actually seeking to facilitate the entry of immigrants of a certain type to this country from different lands, then we should at the same time make it as easy as possible for these people to be able to carry out what they desire to do provided they meet our standards.
One of the biggest problems of the immigrant is to find out what he has to do in getting a passport, satisfying the medical requirements, exchanging his money, meeting the various conditions that must be met, and obtaining his transportation. In so far as there is set forth a clear policy that can be interpreted, and at the moment we have none, then it should be interpreted in practical results at the other end in a way that will assist those who are seeking to come here. There is no difficulty whatever about bringing together under one roof in every great centre through which immigrants will pass all the facilities that will make it possible for them to arrange to come here without having to go all over the place in a large city which they are perhaps visiting for the first time. This has been done, and although it is not being done today it can be done by our own department of immigration. The administration of every one of these various requirements can be brought into a single office so that immigrants can come in, pass their tests, be examined, and have that office provide everything for them, including transportation. That would then facilitate arrangements at this end for meeting them and helping them to find their new homes. May I briefly refer to the Prime Minister's suggestion that it took very little

Citizenship and Immigration to satisfy some people. That was very noisily demonstrated following his remarks at that point. I must say that I hope no embarrassment will be caused his supporters by reason of the fact that he is now taking the very excellent advice of two newspapers about which some of his supporters in Ontario have not been so complimentary in the past.
I wish to refer seriously, however, to one aspect of the creation of a Department of Citizenship and Immigration and the placing of these matters under another minister. I deferred these comments because I had just been informed of something that emphasizes a point I wish to make, and that I attempted to make in my earlier remarks on second reading. To whatever extent this country is prepared to receive immigrants from other lands, then in this complex period in the development of our modern society we should not ask those immigrants when they arrive here to work out their own problems without adequate assistance in regard to those things about which almost inevitably they will know nothing at all. I mentioned previously the desirability of simplifying the procedure at the other end so that when people go to London, Paris, Rome or any other large city in Europe, perhaps for the very first time, they may find that in one place they will be able to carry out all the details that are necessary for them to come to their new home.
More than that is needed, however. When they arrive here it is not enough that they simply be handed booklets telling of our currency provisions, giving a map of the country, and certain explanations of our habits and customs. It is essential that we set up an effective mechanism to really help these people find themselves in the places where they can get the kind of work for which they are suited by their past experience. This is particularly true in the case of those who do not speak either English or French. In those cases it is essential that adequate provision be made to inform those people in their own language exactly what they must do in order to find suitable occupations.
Just today I saw an illustration of this point which emphasizes the need for carrying our whole immigration and citizenship machinery further than it has yet gone. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police have investigated a report from Thessalon that six Italian immigrants were left for 29 days, without proper food or clothing, in a broken-down lumber camp 70 miles north of that northern Ontario centre. This press dispatch further indicates that the Ontario provincial police had investigated this situation first, and had explained that these people 

were wholly unprepared to meet the conditions which confronted them. It is reported that the deputy minister of lands and forests in Ontario said that these men were apparently completely inexperienced with Canadian bush conditions, and the food they took into the camp was not enough for the hard work to be performed. As a result of this, the men nearly starved.
Incidents of this type are happening too often. They are happening because there is no machinery set up to effectively guide these people; not to say what they must do, but to assist them in finding the sort of work for which they are suited. They should be helped to equip themselves to meet the conditions they are going to meet. This applies not only to the people coming from the lands I have mentioned, but also to those whom we describe as d.p.'s. Those d.p.'s have gone through experiences that justify every consideration on our part. If these people have satisfied our tests as to admissibility, then the very kind of experience through which they have passed will give them reason to be among our best citizens, so long as we receive them well when they come here. From their own experience, those people know what freedom really means. Except for those who are deliberately planted here as communist agents, they are the most vigorous anti-communists we shall have in our community, so long as we really welcome them with an effective procedure of assistance when they arrive here. I strongly urge that, with the creation of this new department, we have an efficient and businesslike system for helping those whom we are going to receive in Canada.
We should receive them without the slightest suggestion of directing either their work or how they will live. We should assist them, not only in getting to places where the type of work for which they are qualified will be available, but also in meeting the conditions they will face, particularly if they are far from the settled communities to which they are accustomed. We are fighting communism, and everything for which it stands, on the wider field. Most of those who come here from other countries are coming because of their belief in freedom. One of the ways in which we shall most effectively make sure that they continue to believe in freedom and our democratic system, so that they will become the excellent type of citizens for which their background fits them if they have an opportunity, is to help them when they arrive, to encourage them in every way to feel that we are really welcoming them as citizens of Canada. This procedure would

prevent any poisoning by communist doctrines, and would make them good citizens once they have decided to make this their home.

Mr. Chairman, if I may I should like to obtain clarification of the position of the Indians and Eskimos in Newfoundland. I believe the Prime Minister will recall that I addressed a question to him the other day, but I did not expect an answer at that time because he was not prepared to give it. There are a number of questions arising out of preliminary statements that were obtained in 1947. If it is permissible, I should like to have those questions answered now.
In 1947, sir, there was a meeting between the delegation from the Newfoundland national convention and a committee of the cabinet. A special committee of the delegates and of the committee of the cabinet was set up to deal with Indian and Eskimo problems. A preliminary statement showing the position of Newfoundland Indians and Eskimos in the event of union can be found on page 102 of volume 2 of the report of meetings by the delegates from the national convention of Newfoundland and representatives of the government of Canada. It states:
Under the Indian. Act, Indians and Eskimos in Canada are regarded as one race for purposes of administration. In the event of Newfoundland becoming a province of Canada, the Indians and Eskimos of Newfoundland and Labrador would be the sole responsibility of the federal government and, under existing legislation, would be entitled to benefits and would be subject to regulations which include the following:
I am not going through them all, but I shall deal with the pertinent ones. No. 1 reads as follows:
Free education, provided through day schools and boarding schools. Where boarding schools already exist subsidies ranging from $165 to $300 per pupil per year are paid.
I should like to know if that is so.
2.	Free medical services including hospitalization.
I know that cannot be correct because I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare a question at page 2149 of Hansard. His answer is as follows:
While the federal government has given some assistance in emergency cases provision of medical services for the Indians and Eskimos in Labrador has been and has continued to be the responsibility of the Newfoundland government.
There is a definite contradiction on that particular point.
At page 103 of the volume from which I have been quoting, it is stated that the provincial governments in Canada do not contribute in any way to the support of the Indian population.
Citizenship and Immigration
I continue to quote from the report of the meeting between the delegates from Newfoundland and the cabinet:
3.	Family allowances on the same basis as white population and applied in the normal way wherever possible.
I believe those allowances are paid, but I do not know how.
4.	Land reserves for settlements and trapping lines are set up, by arrangements with the provincial government.
I do not believe any such provision has been made.
5.	Free conservation projects, fishing projects, handicrafts and other aids are undertaken in their behalf.
I do not believe anything has been done in that connection.
6.	The federal government sets up trading posts, where there are no satisfactory arrangements for trading by private interests. This is done to help Indians eventually to buy and market co-operatively themselves.
I shall not refer to the other matters of land tax, income tax, or their right to use intoxicating liquors; I think that is natural.
Indians do not receive old age pensions but relief for the aged is provided.
That is the statement we were given in 1947. I do not know whether the position has changed since that time, but I feel certain from what I have heard that many of these provisions have not become effective. It may be through an inability to carry them out, but I would appreciate the Prime Minister or the Minister of Mines and Resources clarifying the position, if that is a fair question, because I have received some questions about the matter.

I want to say just a word in support of the idea advanced by the leader of the opposition. I refer to the treatment of d.p.'s after they have come to this country. First, however, I want to pay my respects to those concerned and to convey my thanks for the courtesy and fairness with which I have always been treated by Mr. Jolliffe and Mr. Smith in the offices down there; but there is an incident that I wish to mention, and it is one which I have heard is duplicated in many places.
I refer to the unkind treatment which people not familiar with our language are receiving in some of our offices. In Calgary we have a fine man at the head of the office, and he is doing a splendid job. I know that the department cannot carry to all its employees the idea that they should be purveyors of peace, light and justice; but in that


office a certain incident occurred. I speak of this particular case because it concerns a d.p. woman who came out here and happened to get a job as a maid in my daughter's house. She could speak no English. She now speaks English quite well. She stayed her year, so there is not a word of criticism about her. Her husband was anxious to join her, and I took some part in arranging that he should come. I had to do that because this woman of about thirty years of age was received in that office with rudeness which was almost brutal. My daughter went down with her, obtained an interpreter and herself received extremely rude treatment there. The papers were thrown at them and they were told "Fill these out, but who is going to pay for it?" and so on. That was none of their business at that moment. I am not blaming anyone in the department but I am making a suggestion. Bear in mind, Mr. Chairman, the effect upon poorer persons, lacking the ability to speak the language, when they are received in that manner. The effect may last throughout the time of their residence in this country.
I have no doubt that bulletins have been issued from the head office but I am making the suggestion that perhaps a little more care should be taken to see that the civil servant who makes the actual contact will be a little bit more patient and will have a little bit more kindness in his soul; because these first impressions made on people of that type may be lasting ones, I fear. I do not intend to discuss communism, but dissatisfaction is the ground in which it grows. It seems to me that we should have some schooling for these people who first make contact with these immigrants who come to our shores.

I thank the hon. member for mentioning this matter. A training in courtesy is given to these employees of the department of immigration. I am told that over 30 million cases have been handled by the officials of that department. That figure surprised me, and I was given this explanation. It includes even our American friends and neighbours who often come here several times. But over a very long period during which 30 million cases have been handled by officers of the department, there have been only fifteen cases in which, discourtesy having been reported and investigations having been made, it was found that the facts required a reprimand to the official concerned.
But I think that any Canadian who knows of any case of discourteous treatment in circumstances such as those referred to by the hon. member for Calgary West would be doing a service to Canada by bringing it to the attention of the department here. We

all realize that the impressions made by our public servants on those who come here either as immigrants or as visitors should be a good one, in keeping with the mentality and the habits of the Canadian people. Those who represent the Canadian people in the contacts of officialdom with immigrants or visitors should give a proper impression of the kind of people Canadians are. When any of them do not do that, I think it would be a service to have the conduct of the delinquent brought to the attention of the department for which he acts, so that the circumstances may be investigated and a repetition prevented.

I can assure the hon. member that, if it were found that placing the health service for the Indians in this department would cut down the expense, that would be done; but the advice we got was that there would be less duplication by having these health services administered by the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
