subtopic: PROVISION FOR MODIFICATION OF CURRENT AND FUTURE CONTRACTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am happy to comply with my hon. friend's wish. In presenting the resolution I stated that the principle behind it was greater simplicity and flexibility in administration. Certain doubts have arisen as to the existence of statutory authority in the act as it now stands for the putting into effect of some things which ordinary business and agricultural practice would indicate to be desirable and to be in the best interests of veterans under the act and the country at large. The proposed changes are for the purpose of removing these doubts, and also to permit the administration to cope with certain conditions which did not exist, and could not have been easily anticipated, when the act was originally framed. As hon. members will recall, that was back in 1942. Probably the most important improvements proposed by this bill are those designed to permit the director to effect the sale of property on behalf of a veteran, and to permit the redisbursement of the sale proceeds for the purchase of other property, or for improvements to the veteran's property when that appears to be in the best interests of the veteran and when at the same time it will improve or maintain the security under the contract. The changes proposed will make it legally possible to carry out normal business transactions, and will assist the veteran in the improvement of his property; and consequently, of course, will improve his chances of success.
The bill provides ample safeguards against transactions of a purely speculative nature. A sale and substitution, where the whole property is involved, will not be permitted more than once. Any surplus created as a result of the transaction will be applied to reduce the veteran's debt. Sales will be made only on a cash basis, except where the director requires the property for the settlement of another veteran and the first veteran is willing to part with it at its appraised value. For example, the bill will make possible the disposal of matured trees, surplus buildings, sand, gravel or minerals and reinvestment of the proceeds in improvements such as new buildings, fences, the clearing of land and so on. It will enable the sale of part of a property, not well suited to the enterprise, and the purchase of more suitable adjoining land, thereby improving the veteran's unit. It will permit the sale of the entire property where it is found unsuitable
or where the veteran has been moved by his employer to another part of the country, and the use of the proceeds for the purchase of another property suited to the veteran's needs and requirements. It is believed that this will do much to improve and round out properties, and will make it possible for a veteran settled under the act to continue his settlement when and where circumstances make a move to another locality imperative or desirable.
Somewhat related to the first proposal mentioned is one which will permit the director to release to a veteran part of a property which, at the time of the contract with the veteran, represented value substantially in excess of that required to protect the director's investment. This situation exists of course, where the veteran made a substantial payment of his own money at the time the property was purchased, or where the veteran had a sizeable equity in the property for one reason or another before he approached the Veterans Land Act for assistance. The bill will permit the release to a veteran, at his request, of that part of a property which represented surplus value in excess of the price paid at the time the property was purchased.
I know a number of hon. members have received complaints from veterans who have been unable to secure refunds consequent upon the sale of their properties at prices equal to or greater than the sale prices to the veterans. As explained to the veterans so affected, the trouble here lay not with the administration but in the wording of the act. I am sure hon. members will be glad to learn, therefore, that changes here proposed will remove the legal difficulties which exist in that regard.
Hon. members will also recall that in order to have as many homes as possible ready and available for our service men and women on their return from overseas, an extensive building program on small holding project properties was inaugurated early in 1945. Owing to conditions which existed at that time the cost of these houses, including the necessary remedial work which was much discussed in this house, was substantially higher that what was considered to be their true value. To ensure that these houses would be available to veterans as soon as completed and at a fair price, cabinet approval was given for their sale at a price which would represent value rather than cost, such price to be fixed by a committee composed of the deputy minister of my department and the director of the Veterans Land Act. After these sales were made

Veterans Land Act
questions arose as to the validity of this procedure and of contracts made in accordance with it. One of the proposals in this bill, therefore, is for the purpose of curing this possible deficiency and of ensuring that veterans who hold agreements for sale for properties, the sale price of which was less than cost to the director, may be given a good and sufficient title in accordance with the terms of their existing contracts.
The other changes proposed are mainly for the purpose of removing any doubts that may have arisen as to the exact meaning of some sections of the act, and to broaden the scope of some sections which experience has shown to be unnecessarily restrictive.
Hon. members, of course, are fully aware of the ramifications of the land settlement operations carried on under the Veterans Land Act and, I am sure, will all the more readily appreciate that the act as originally enacted could not have been designed to meet all contingencies which might arise during those operations. I might add here that these amendments are brought forward by the administration, of course in co-operation with the veterans most vitally concerned as well as the veteran community and those interested in agriculture generally, to provide a greater flexibility in the administration of the act. As may be expected, since the act was passed in 1942 experience has shown the need for supplementary provisions to cope with many real problems; and it is to the solution of these problems that this legislation is mainly directed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MODIFICATION OF CURRENT AND FUTURE CONTRACTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has taken a short time to explain this bill, and I think has made its purpose clear to most of us. He said the object of the legislation was to give the administration of the act greater simplicity, and that he thought these amendments were in the best interests of our veterans. He also said that the act as originally adopted did not meet all the contingencies that have arisen since. That, of course, is true of most veteran legislation. We have found as time has gone by that practically all the veteran legislation needed to be amended at some time or other.
For this reason, as I have stated in this house on previous occasions, I feel there is great need for a committee on veterans affairs. I offer no apology for bringing up this matter again, though I have mentioned it already on a good many occasions. I do not think any committee of this house could do better work, or any committee in the past has done better work, than a committee on veterans affairs. If these contingencies that arise all the time could be discussed in such a committee, and if suggested amendments

to legislation could receive such consideration, I think they would be given far more attention than is possible here, in the last days of the session. That may not have been as necessary in connection with this legislation as in connection with other acts, but I think the general principle is sound. So I hope when another session is called the government and the minister will agree that it is advisable to set up this committee.
The minister said that new difficulties were arising all the time, in spite of the elaborate set-up we have spreading all over the country. I agree with that statement. For instance, while I believe our educational program has been a great success, we all know that some men who attended universities probably would have been much better off on farms, or taking technical training. If a man wishes to take up some other work than that in which he is now engaged, this act makes provision for him to do so. I have no doubt there are many men who went on farms who have found that they would have been better engaged in other work. I believe the act makes provision for meeting this contingency as well.
While I was going through the act, I noted many points. For instance, there is a new provision in this act so far as eligibility is concerned. Provision is made for a man to change his locality. The act was rather rigid previously, and the man who took a small holding in Toronto or some other city, then found he was transferred to Ottawa, Halifax, or Saint John, found himself in difficulty. Arrangements can be made now, however, for him to sell his property in Toronto and purchase another in Halifax.
The minister spoke about the small holdings. Frankly, I think most of the trouble with the Veterans Land Act has been in the small holdings branch of that department. I remember there were grave doubts in the committee as to whether the Department of Veterans Affairs should go into the housing business. As the minister has pointed out, there was a scarcity of houses. A great number of returned men were looking for houses, and this practically compelled the Department of Veterans Affairs to undertake the housing proposition. There has been a lot of criticism of these small holdings, especially from veterans who took up properties near large cities, who found that the minimum of one-half acre was not satisfactory. I believe this fact, in itself, has kept a great many veterans from establishing themselves under the small holdings provisions of the Veterans Land Act. I believe that is something which could be investigated by the minister's department.

I was interested in reading a report of the Department of Veterans Affairs for 1948. It contains one paragraph which I think sets out this problem quite well. It says:
The agricultural development of small holdings along the lines visualized by parliament is a responsibility challenging the best efforts of the administration.
I have no doubt that the efforts of the administration have been well challenged, but there is a grave question in the minds of the people of this country as to whether this challenge has been met.
Involving as it does the development of a new way of life and its integration into the economic and social set-up. very careful thought and planning is necessary, and follow-up over a long period is essential for success. Results to date are most encouraging in spite of the fact that to many settlers the acquisition of a small holding was, in the first instance, only with the idea of getting themselves a home.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that was the main idea in the mind of a great many veterans. I feel also that there were many veterans who, having a permanent job of some type, felt they would like to carry on some farming activity on the side. At first they were quite enthusiastic, but they found there were other obligations which interfered with it. Some of them found they would like to entertain themselves at some amusement, such as ball games, playing golf, and so on. On many of these small holdings it will be found that, while a small garden has been put into operation, much of the land is not being used at all. I believe the act does provide that, if a man has too much land, he can sell part of it through the board to someone else who desires to build on it.
There was another matter which was frequently mentioned in our committee, and that was the legal costs to the veteran, and the long delay which was often experienced in transferring property. In some cases it was thought that the costs were too great. In certain localities a few lawyers seemed to have a virtual monopoly on this work for which they obtained large fees. I believe the minister's department should carefully investigate this matter to ensure that, so far as the local end of these transfers is concerned, they are put through as quickly as possible.
Another point which should be mentioned, which has a bearing on this situation, is not so much a problem of the veterans affairs department as of the postmaster general. I have received complaints from men who have settled on veterans' farms, as well as other people in the locality, that the lack of a daily mail service was keenly felt. I know that veterans are often inclined to leave a community in the country in which it is impossible to have a proper mail service. As
Veterans Land Act
I say, this is not the responsibility of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, but I hope he will take it up with his colleagues. Neither a farmer nor any other person living in this country should have a poor mail service. I believe the post office system is out of date. The Post Office Department demands that there be four persons per mile before giving a daily service. This regulation is reacting against many of the people living in the country, as well as against many of our returned men.
I do not think there is anything further I wish to say, Mr. Speaker. I do give the bill general approval, and I think it will correct a good many mistakes and shortcomings in the old legislation. I shall close on the same note on which I started, and that is that, while there are not so many veterans' problems to be brought to the attention of the house now, still the veterans of this country feel they are entitled to a standing committee of this house. This would enable the veterans in the house to deal with veterans' problems. Bills such as this, upon being brought before this House of Commons, would be referred to this committee and given careful consideration.

Mr. Speaker, in 1946 section 9 of the Veterans Land Act, 1942, was repealed and a new section 9 inserted. It set forth the conditions under which veterans could receive assistance in setting themselves up on the land, and providing themselves with the necessary equipment. This loan is repayable over a period not to exceed 25 years.
There is one matter in this connection which I desire to bring to the attention of the minister. Perhaps it applies solely to my own province of Saskatchewan. In that province farms of large acreage have been springing up on a co-operative basis. Some of them are managed entirely by groups of veterans. I understand that the individual veteran on such a farm has been able to receive his grant; that is to say, as an individual, even though he is part of the co-operative enterprise, but apparently the veteran on a co-operative farm is not entitled to the loan other veterans receive who buy a farm upon an individual basis. My plea to the minister is that the act should be amended so that this condition would be changed. The aid in the form of loans now available to the individual should be available to the individual even when he has partners in the enterprise. In Saskatchewan there are large acreages of land which are now available; and when I say there is land available, I mean improved farms. There are farms there running into one or two thousand acres; after all a farm of sixteen

Veterans Land Act
hundred acres is not exceptional in Saskatchewan. These farms are too valuable to be purchased by the average individual; and at any rate they represent an acreage too great to be taken care of by a single purchaser. I think some of these farms could form the basis of the kind of co-operative enterprises that I have described and which have already been set up, and could be purchased by groups of veterans so inclined, provided that they have the necessary financial resources. My plea to the government is that this money should be available to these people so that they could purchase such farms. I know that the soundness of the security is a matter of importance to the government. I think, however, that the soundness of the security would not be impaired but rather enhanced by any such arrangement, by carrying out the co-operative idea rather than the idea of individual ownership.
These veterans could establish themselves under favourable conditions with partners of their own choosing who would be congenial to them. The overhead expenses of these farms could be cut down, as they are now being cut down on those which have been established on the same basis, by the assistance which they could give one another in their work and by the use of machinery owned in common. A congenial social life-something which, by the way, is important in those large areas, having regard to the climate we have, particularly in the winter-would be available, something which is now impossible on the average individual farm. That is one of the reasons why some of our rural population in Saskatchewan spend most of their winters in the nearest town. They want to enjoy the company of others of their own kind.
I mention these matters because I believe they should appeal to the government from the point of view of an enhanced rather than a lessened security for the return of the money lent, as well as from the point of view of rehabilitation of veterans under favourable conditions, thus affording an additional prospect of success. I am sure that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) has had many cases of men breaking down under certain conditions-solitude and plugging along alone -whereas groups of men, following the old tradition of the army, get along a good deal better if they are surrounded by some of their buddies. I think that this matter might be the subject of discussion in a committee on veterans affairs, and I should like to back up the plea of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) that such a committee be set up and that that be one of the subjects referred to it.
rMr. Knight.]
In this connection, I may say that there is a man who I think could be useful to such a committee as a witness. He is Mr. Chapman, who is now director of co-operative farming in Saskatchewan. I believe the Canadian Legion in Saskatchewan and the co-operative farm conference have gone on record as favouring this particular proposal of mine. The minister may know-and he can tell us if he will-whether representations have been made to him, and to what extent such representations have been made to him in this regard. At any rate, that is my plea. I hope the government will give consideration to this matter of making these loans under the act available to veterans farming or wishing to farm on a co-operative basis.

Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I was not in the chamber when the minister spoke; I was attending a meeting of a committee. But I may say that, generally speaking, I am in favour of the amendments contained in this bill, although it appears to me that as a result of these amendments we are possibly getting further and further away from the original purpose of the Veterans Land Act, having regard to veterans and small holdings. The original idea was to settle a veteran on a small holding, with a house, so that he might use that land in order to supplement his income. As a result of these amendments he may perhaps dispose of the land and just have the house left. That certainly was not the original intention of the Veterans Land Act. Nevertheless, if it is to the benefit of the veteran to do that, I personally would not object.
To me there appears to be some confusion in these amendments as to whether or not a veteran is entitled to recover his down payment when land is sold. We shall, however, have a chance to ask questions on that point when we get into committee on the sections.
There is one other point that I hope the minister will be able to discuss, although perhaps it really does not come under this bill. It is the matter of whether or not veterans may be eligible for the grant when they settle on crown lands; and I am speaking particularly of the special areas. I have taken this matter up with the department on several occasions but so far have not been able to get a satisfactory answer. I have been told that the matter is under discussion. In view of the fact that last spring letters were written stating that a certain decision had been reached, and that action would be forthcoming in the near future, I hope that the minister will be able to clarify that point.

Just before the house goes into committee, Mr. Speaker, may I say I do not think that the motion for

second reading of this bill should pass without somebody saying a word in appreciation, first, of the legislation itself and, second, of the manner in which it has been administered by the department under the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg). I do not think any words of mine could describe the fine results that have been achieved under this legislation better than the figures, which I should like to put on Hansard, as to the actual number of houses which have been built under the Veterans Land Act in the various areas of Canada.
Under the individual housing program of the Veterans Land Act, up to September 30, 1949-and this will be the date for all the provinces that I will mention-in Nova Scotia 313 houses were built; in Prince Edward Island, 96; in New Brunswick, 364; in Quebec, 921; in eastern Ontario, 2,419; in western Ontario, 1,931; in Manitoba, 474; in Saskatchewan, 203; in Alberta, 725; and in British Columbia, 1,304. In the providing of adequate inexpensive housing for the veterans of this country I think that is an achievement of which this parliament and the government can be justly proud. I did not think it was proper that the motion for the second reading of the amendments to this act should pass without something being said in this regard.
While I am on my feet I should like to comment on two or three of the observations of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks). He stated that in his opinion the department had had a great deal of trouble with small holdings. I believe it is true that certain troubles were experienced; but the department, the minister and the responsible officers did not shrink from those troubles. The manner in which they were met has in great part been responsible for the tremendous success of this legislation.
In addition the hon. member repeated the argument that there should be a committee on veterans affairs. All members of the house who were here at the second to last session of the last parliament will remember the work done by the veterans affairs committee at that time, and also the work done by previous sessional committees on veterans affairs. The day may come when a sessional committee may have to be set up; but I do think there is no need at the present time for a permanent standing committee on veterans affairs. I for one approve of the government's decision not to take that step.
It does seem to me that these repeated urgings from the official opposition for the setting up of various permanent committees indicate that there must be in that party a feeling that we should get away from the

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the house for long, but I do wish to give my support to this bill and the amendments it proposes to the Veterans Land Act. I am pleased to note that the Department of Veterans Affairs, particularly, is willing to bring in amendments arising from experience, with a view to making legislation work to the better advantage of the veterans. I should hope that some other departments of government might learn a lesson from the Department of Veterans Affairs and recommend amendments to legislation when such legislation does not work out satisfactorily, or requires amendment.
I would support the proposal of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) that at the next session of the house we have a special committee on veterans affairs. As the hon. member has said, I believe that is the wish of all the major veterans organizations in this country, and such a committee would play a useful part in assisting the government in the further development of veteran legislation.
I am pleased to see these amendments because I believe they will be beneficial to some men in my constituency. I have known of men taking up some holdings under the act, and then having to transfer their employment, or having to transfer their locations of residence because of health reasons, employment reasons, or for some other unforeseen cause. For that reason I am sure these amendments will assist a great many veterans in Canada and correct a situation which requires correction.
I could not take my seat without again emphasizing my hope, and the hope of the veterans I represent, that the government will see fit in the near future to reduce small holdings to half an acre, and make it possible for thousands of veterans to take advantage of this excellent legislation. I am pleased, too, to see the qualifications for application under the act extended to this

Veterans Land Act
group of pensioners who are pensioned on account of disability received in any theatre of service.
That is all I have to say at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this section. I did not say anything when Mr. Speaker was in the chair, because there were certain questions I wanted to ask.
In my view this is a good bill, and makes the act more workable than it was before. It does raise certain questions, but before going into those I should like to comment on the general principle of these small holdings, and the idea behind them when the act was passed in 1942. Many hon. members here today served on that committee, and they will know that the idea of small holdings as it was put forth at that time was not intended as a housing scheme. It was only after the veterans began to come back from overseas, and the scarcity of houses developed, that the scheme became a housing scheme. It seems to me there is a difference between the two, but that as yet the department has not been able to resolve that difference.
There is a demand for housing and a demand for small holdings. In between the two we have many holdings the classification of which it is difficult to define. I believe the department will continue to have difficulty until there is some amendment in the act to distinguish between veterans housing and small holdings. The setting up of that division may offer some difficulty. However, unless there is some division there will always be that marginal ground where it will be difficult to decide what veterans should do with their holdings-whether they should be able to dispose of part of them, or whether they should be retained as part of the holding of the veterans.
The veteran now on a small holding may sell part of that holding. There are many veterans who have holdings of two or three acres. If they subdivide and sell part of those holdings, immediately there will be a demand on the part of veterans coming in under the act to get holdings smaller than the two or three acres available at the present time. What is the position to be in that connection?
If under this amendment to the act the subdividing of a small holding is allowed, then quite rightly other veterans who may
[Mr. Herrldge.l
be coming under the act will ask for smaller holdings. They will ask for a reduction to the half-acre holdings.
I should like also to say a word with respect to the matter raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon. That is a problem we are going to meet in certain parts of Canada as time goes on, the matter of large farms going on the market for sale. In my own constituency I know of several large farms of five, six or seven sections, in good areas which, because of the desire of the owners to retire, are going on the market. It is good land; but no single veteran can hope to purchase that amount of land. Where a group of veterans wish to get together to form a co-operative in order to farm some land that might become available under section 9, they could purchase it and operate it more successfully than they could as individuals. I think some consideration should be given to amending the act to allow that development to take place. It is a natural development that is going on and if it is successful I think it should be encouraged. I have some other questions with regard to other sections which I shall bring up later.

In dealing with the questions that have been asked under this section perhaps I may take the last first and then deal with the others. The hon. member for Melfort, the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Royal have all referred to the idea behind these small holdings. I should like to make it abundantly clear that there is no withdrawal from the original idea. It is true that in the days of demobilization in 1945 and 1946, when it was more vital even than it is now to get demobilized men under cover, an amendment was made by order in council to the regulations of that day to permit the obtaining of blocks of land in the vicinity of large centres and breaking them into half-acre lots which became known as projects or subdivisions. A good deal of difficulty was experienced in getting equipment and skilled help to build the houses for these lots. After looking over the record I am free to state that the motive of having a small place in which to live in the country did not at that time carry a great deal of weight. In 1946, I believe, that was reversed and the regulations went back to two and three acres where it now stands.
The value of the original small holding idea has been pointed out this afternoon. I think we are beginning to come to a realization of it. Some hon. members may have seen reports of a competition which the director conducted within the last twelve months, for small holdings both in subdivisions and on individual settlements across the country. That, as well as many other things, including the remedial steps taken with regard to houses, helped to raise greatly the morale of many veterans settled under this provision of the act. During the present month, while things are reasonably quiet in the work of the administration of the Veterans Land Act, there is being carried

Veterans Land Act
on in Ottawa what I tell the director is a young college. Senior men and their assistants from every section of Canada are taking a three-weeks course. Those providing instruction in that course are drawn from many fields of activities having to do with agriculture, horticultural and small holdings. Now that we have had the plan back on the two and three acre plan for a goodly period, it is evident that there is great and continuing interest in this particular way of life that was visualized in 1942 when the smallholding idea came into effect.
For instance, let us take the first year, 1945-46. Approved applications for small holdings numbered 2,318. I admit the war ended that year, and consequently it took a little while for veterans to decide what they wanted to do, but in the first six months of the 1949-50 year there have been 1,808 approved applications for small holdings. If it continues on the same basis there will be 3,616 this year, or a good many more than the first year of demobilization. Of course the same thing can be stated as to those going on dominion and provincial lands. The rise there has been much more marked because it took some little time to get under way.
The other point which was made by most members who spoke was an expression of concern whether the provision under this section for the sale of a part of the property might result in its being reduced to a very small lot. The answer is no. The director will only have authority to allow the veteran to sell a portion of his property when the remaining portion is not less than the amount he would otherwise be required to have. It does not change the acreage position in any way whatsoever.

Perhaps that was all right in theory when we started, but in practice it is working a hardship on those who are obliged to move through no fault of their own. For example, I have in mind a case where a soldier working for an oil company established himself on that basis, and then was ordered to another part of the country after being there for three or four years. He is placed in the position that he has to refund the 25 per cent, and thus loses the benefit of that particular provision of the act. Mr. Speaker, when the house was considering this bill a week ago I had not quite concluded my remarks. I suggest to you and to hon. members of the house that the test which should be applied to these private bills granting charters to build a pipe line should be this: Is the proposed company going to give the greatest possible service to the Canadian people?
The company under discussion in this bill, to be known as the Alberta Natural Gas Company, does not meet that test. The proposal is to run a pipe line from southern Alberta, through the Crowsnest pass and thence into the United States. We are told that they hope to bring it out again at the end to serve Vancouver, which would then be at the end of the line. It should be made perfectly clear that that plan means that this company will serve, first, the interiors of Idaho, Washington and possibly Oregon; second, the United States west coast cities of Seattle, Tacoma and Portland; and, third and last, the Canadian west coast will be able to get whatever surplus is left.
I have here this week's issue of V.S. News and World Report. The heading of the article to which I am referring is, "Canada: Oil's new hot spot." A map appears with the article illustrating the oil boom now at flood
tMr. Gregg.]

The first interest of this company is the Pacific northwest states, not the province of British Columbia.
Since I made my speech last week the Vancouver Sun of November 24, 1945, has arrived which contains an article datelined at Calgary and reading as follows:
Northwest Natural Gas Company has asked the Alberta natural gas and conservation board for an adjournment of its hearing for permission to export gas to points outside the province.
I point out that that is an application made to the Alberta authorities by the Northwest Natural Gas Company. The article continues:
This company, which has plans to bring Alberta's gas to the coast by a southerly route through the United States, has run into difficulty in the House of Commons, in its move to get federal approval for incorporation.
Previous to this sitting of the house it had requested Alberta to hear its application on November 28. Now the application might not come up until after the end of the year.
They are waiting to get this bill through the house.
British Columbia's government and many residents have gone on record supporting Westcoast. A line through northern British Columbia and Alberta would build up the sparsely settled districts in both provinces, they say.
There is no doubt at all who is behind this application for a charter. It is a United States company which is planning to serve the northwestern states. I suggest that the line should be through British Columbia to the coast, and I do not care which route it follows provided that it goes through Canadian territory. If there is any surplus it can then be sent on to United States west coast cities. Nobody could have any objection to that.

If that plan were followed, instead of this pipe line serving the interior of the northwest Pacific states, the American Pacific coast cities and finally the west coast of Canada, we would have the interior of British Columbia served first, then Canadian west coast centres and finally United States west coast cities, if any surplus was available. I need only point out to hon. members that when we were discussing the trans-Canada highway this week everyone insisted that it should go through Canada; no one suggested anything else. Surely we should do the same thing with this natural gas pipe line.
I suggest that some delay is advisable before a decision is reached on this point. A question like this should not be settled in the dying days of this short session; time should be available to determine how Canadians can best be served by this pipe line. Then thought should also be given to having placed in the charters the route to be followed. I repeat the argument I made before, that there should be written right into the charter where the company has to lay out its route. Further, an attempt should be made to negotiate with the United States. If this ripe line or other pipe lines have to cross the boundary and then come back into Canada, we have no assurance they will come back unless there is a treaty with the United States. It is ridiculous to leave it to a private company to make the arrangements. Once the pipe line crosses our boundary we lose all control, and the only way we can get any control at all is by having a treaty.
I also believe consideration should be given to writing more controls into the dominion legislation. There should be some method of controlling the rates to be charged by the pipe line companies. At the present time there is practically no control over a natural gas pipe line under the dominion Pipe Lines Act. Time should be taken for public opinion to crystallize on the broad question. It involves more than natural gas and oil. We shall be faced with the same decision in connection with our iron ore in Quebec and Labrador. There is a great issue to be settled by the Canadian people. My party and I believe in conserving Canadian resources for the use of the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some two weeks ago in the house when we were discussing a resolution presented by the hon. member for Eglinton, in which he asked for a committee on health, a debate on health matters ensued. At that time we had an opportunity to discuss matters of health in Canada. Unfortunately the Minister of National Health and Welfare was not in his seat at the time, because he was absent on other important business.
The opportunity to speak on health matters is usually limited to three or four hours toward the close of the session; yet it is one of the most important matters debated in the House of Commons. During the debate on the resolution offered by the hon. member for Eglinton I placed before the house certain
2626	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Health and Welfare important statistics showing the state of national health in Canada, and suggested certain remedies for that condition.
There is no occasion to repeat the statistics I gave at that time, but the brief summary I placed on record concerning our national health served to show that the picture at the present time is not reassuring. I pointed out the change that had taken place in the last two or three decades in respect of the principal causes of death. I attempted to show that the diseases which formerly headed the list as causes of mortality had changed, and that such diseases as old age, heart disease and cancer were now at the top of the list, and were the leading causes of death in this country.
The diseases I have mentioned should have the attention of all workers in the field of public health. While they may not contribute to a rise in the mortality rate they offer a challenge to the research workers of this country.
In a previous debate I mentioned the prevalence of mental diseases and drew attention to the shortage of hospital beds for these cases. We could also debate other matters such as sewage disposal, contamination of water and so on. These are important matters that should be brought before this house. I drew attention to the need for more housing space, the necessity for the rehabilitation of disabled persons, the high accident rate in this country; these are things that should be discussed when national health matters are being considered.
There are no statistics available with regard to the rehabilitation of disabled persons, but we can take into consideration tubercular cases released from sanitaria, cardiac or heart cases, the blind and the enormous number of those mentally afflicted, and those who have been physically handicapped by accident or disease. Many of these people are invalids who require care and support, and in spite of the progress we have made in finding new ways to rehabilitate those who are handicapped, they still pose a problem. We still have many obstacles to overcome and there is still much to do.
We do not feel that the situation is entirely hopeless because new weapons are now available in the fight against disease and suffering and we have every reason to believe that national health can be raised to a level higher than that which exists at the present time. If each province and the dominion take the proper steps to put into force and use the new knowledge acquired from research in the last twenty years, the condition in so far as this country is concerned will be corrected. But it will require sound planning, it will require


adequate financial support, it will require courageous leadership, and it will require above all the active application of the products of research. There is no doubt that there has been marked improvement in the health of this country. As each province has control of its own health matters we should congratulate the leaders of those provinces upon the splendid improvement that has been brought about in recent years.
As I have pointed out several times, there are two matters which should be kept constantly before us in the consideration of health matters. The first is the necessity of opportunity for treatment and the second is the urgent necessity of applying the results of research, whether in the matter of treatment, hospitalization or prevention. The opportunity to procure treatment in the early stages of a disease is most important. Hospitalization is often beyond the means of a large part of our population.
The cost of hospital accommodation has increased greatly in the last three or four years, although there were signs of increased cost during the war. There has been an increased tendency for people to seek hospital treatment. This is a most expensive item in the budget of every family. There is a reason for this in the fact that it is difficult to obtain help or nursing services in the home. Any one of us can picture the financial blow it is to one of moderate means when faced with a large bill for hospital treatment and accommodation.
This sort of treatment is more expensive for certain types of disease and the facilities for hospital treatment that we have are inadequate to cope with the emergency which exists at the present time. Hospital accommodation is particularly inadequate in the case of mental diseases, tuberculosis and incurables. At the present time many incurables are occupying beds in public wards of hospitals. It is true that they are receiving care and treatment, but our hospitals are short of accommodation and these people are occupying beds which are urgently needed for acute cases.
While the results of research in the last decade have accomplished wonderful things it should be pointed out that some of the newer types of treatment are very expensive, but even though that may be, it is highly necessary that all our people have the advantage of the new products of research. The new product cortisone for the treatment of arthritis, a disease which has been referred to in this house many times and we are watching with interest the clinical results of the administration of this drug. We hope that this will prove the answer to arthritis

which has baffled our research workers and which leaves behind a trail of suffering and chronic invalidism.
There are four objectives we should keep in mind. First, the control of infections; second, health education; third, sanitation; and, fourth, preventive services. In the past those four objectives have produced marvellous results and in order to obtain the best results we should see that those objectives have been attained in every section of our country. In the last four years remarkable progress has been made in health education and it is important in carrying out any scheme for the betterment of health conditions in Canada that our population should be educated, not only in the prevention of disease but on how to take full advantage of early diagnostic measures which may be available to them.
Take cancer as an example. Early signs and symptoms of this disease may often give warning to a patient who has read about it or who has attended lectures and knows something of the symptoms. If he feels that something is wrong he should have an opportunity to attend some clinic or see his own physician and have a proper diagnosis made. Warnings may be noted by a patient at an early date but if they are neglected it means a great deal in the further treatment of the disease.
Voluntary agencies are doing a splendid work in health education. At the present time the Kinsmen are putting on a mass X-ray program in Ottawa and free X-rays are available to the citizens for the diagnosis of tuberculosis. Even though only a few cases of tuberculosis are found, a great work will have been done. These people will be able to seek early treatment, and if they are infectious they will be removed from the population thus hindering further infection by this terrible disease. There may be some variation in the statistics for various parts of the city as to those who are infected, but in so far as the final result is concerned the importance of getting the patient under early treatment in the first stages of the disease cannot be overestimated. I congratulate the Kinsmen or any other service club working in this field.
Poliomyelitis or infantile paralysis is still a problem for research work. We sincerely hope that research in poliomyelitis will advance to the point where we can get control of this terrible, crippling disease. In providing free hospitalization for sufferers from poliomyelitis, my own province of Ontario has been a pioneer in this work. Many of those who might otherwise have been crippled are able to make a complete 45781-167i
Supply-National Health and Welfare recovery owing to hospitalization with physiotherapy and other measures which are used by way of treatment to prevent crippling. It saves a great many of these young people from being permanently crippled.
Over the years it is certainly true that wars have stimulated research, and the means by which lives can be saved have been developed in that time of stress. We have found out a great deal about the treatment of disease, surgery and preventive measures. Even if we had the assurance that there would be no more war, we should intensify our efforts to destroy disease and suffering. I should like to think that some time in the future a healthy world may mean a peaceful world. It is essential that health in our dominion be deemed as important in peace as in wartime.
I cannot discuss these matters without bringing to the attention of hon. members again the increasing number of admissions to mental hospitals. I talked about this matter at the time the other resolution was before the house. I cited statistics and proved to the house that our mental population was increasing faster than our general population. It is most unfortunate that in all the provinces of Canada there is a marked shortage of beds for mental cases. It is a curious fact that mental diseases which cause so much suffering and confusion have received so little attention from preventive medicine until the last few years. Psychiatry is now taking its proper place, and there has been much added to our knowledge and treatment of these diseases. We are now able to provide intensive treatment with excellent results. It is not my purpose to discuss this at this time because it has previously been debated in the house, but there was a time in the treatment of mental disease when all the treatment amounted to was custodial care.
There will always be huge problems to be solved in the field of national health, and as present problems are solved others will arise to take their place. We must be ready to meet any change in situation and to keep pace with the times. We must face the matter realistically day by day, and we must have courage and determination to build for the future in the interests of the people of Canada.
I now come to the question of the administration of the health grants. These were introduced on the 14th of May, 1948, by the former prime minister of this country. I again take issue with the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as I did last year, regarding the manner in which publicity is:
2628	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-National Health and Welfare given to the press and over the radio in connection with these grants, and particularly those to hospitals. Hospitals are now in a serious financial plight, and added to the troubles which they already bear is the serious and alarming shortage of beds. I again point out to the minister that health is primarily a matter within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Over the years it must be admitted that the provinces have done marvellous work in the field of public health, which was mainly accomplished by their own initiative and with their own resources. In the accomplishment of their great work they have done little or no advertising. The work was performed quietly. They felt that the work in the provincial field performed by the departments of health of the various provinces was the job they should be doing.
There are many other agencies which are also responsible for the achievements which have been made up to this time. Certainly not all of the progress made to date has been due to the Department of National Health and Welfare. I again point out to the minister that advertising, no matter in what form it is displayed, has not been part of the traditions of the medical profession, or of any other agency interested in healing. Nurses, physicians and surgeons, hospital executives, and voluntary agencies have toiled over the years in the interests of the people for the elimination of misery and suffering. The minister is learned in another profession, but he has never been schooled in the centuries old traditions of the medical profession and those who have been associated with the science of healing.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that it is becoming distasteful to read and to listen to the publicity given his department which is flaunted before the public as if health departments and health grants had never before existed. I give you an example of this type of publicity. The Globe and Mail of December 1, and I may say most of the other daily papers, but I specially mention this one, carries an article with the headline:
Ottawa grant $560,000, Martin praises hospital.
The Sick Children's Hospital of Toronto is a wonderful institution, and throughout the years has been doing marvellous work in the care of crippled children and those ill from other diseases. There are many people, not only in Toronto and the province of Ontario but also in the whole Dominion of Canada, who are grateful for what has been done for their children by the Toronto Hospital for Sick Children. It has been supported by the city of Toronto and the province of Ontario, and by donations from people throughout the province and the Dominion of Canada who
[Mr. Blair.1
are aware of the great work being done by the institution. They are aware of the wonderful work that has been accomplished in dealing with children, and we are all sympathetic with it.
I understand the cost of the extra accommodation required at the present time will be $12 million. The province of Ontario has made a grant of $2 million. The city of Toronto has made a grant of $1 million, and the Department of National Health and Welfare has made a grant of $560,000. There is a demand, not only in Toronto and Ontario but throughout the whole country, to provide further accommodation. No doubt such accommodation is going to cost a great deal of money. I cited the fact that it will cost about $12 million, but any person reading the headlines which have appeared in the press lately would be led to believe that it was a project of the federal government and of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
It would seem that every grant made by the department for hospital construction is the occasion for a rash of publicity in the press and over the radio. I congratulate the minister on backing up the financial appeal in connection with this hospital. I think it is a very worthy object; but on the other hand I think I have read or heard of every grant given under his administration, either over the radio or in the press. Evidently the minister does not believe in the old scriptural adage of hiding his light under a bushel.
I have not seen any references to the grants given for hospital construction by the province of Ontario, though those grants were in existence before May 15, 1948, when the federal grants were brought in, and are larger than the grants given by this government. While I am speaking on these grants I want to quote from page 6179 of Hansard for June 30, 1948, where the minister was being questioned by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green):

It has become very tiresome to hear all this fanfare and publicity every time a grant is made. It would seem the 'minister has some desire to emulate Little Jack Horner in the children's story, because every time he sticks in his thumb and pulls out a plum he addresses the public and says, "What a good boy am I! Look what I have done!"
When I come to the question of a health policy for Canada, this is part and parcel of the policy of every political party in this house. We may not have the same ideas as to how we are to accomplish it, but we are all striving toward and looking forward to the same objective. The cost of hospitalization is high at the present time, and is becoming very difficult for people to pay. Anyone who has had experience in these matters knows how difficult it is to get a hospital bed even in the city of Ottawa; and this condition exists right across the country. Over the last week end I tried to get a patient into hospital, and I was told that the place was simply jammed and there was no accommodation whatever. It is a serious situation, sir, when a person who is ill and requires hospitalization and treatment is unable to obtain a bed in a hospital.	v
I mentioned the cost a moment ago. It is becoming beyond the means of the average person to pay for hospital care in a public ward, let alone a private room. Take a man in ordinary circumstances, living on his salary and owning his home. If he is faced with the cost of lengthy hospitalization for some member of his family he will probably end up with a mortgage on his house to pay the cost, and will have suffered a financial blow from which he may never recover. It is becoming more and more necessary that we take some forward step to implement some kind of plan that will give relief in this direction.
On political platforms during the last election campaign we heard a great deal about a health plan. We even heard the blame for the absence of that health plan laid on the doorstep of certain provinces. Not only during the period before June 27, but also in the Leeds by-election contest between the Progressive Conservatives and the Toronto Star this was brought prominently to the attention of the people by members of the Liberal party in this house. They were told that the failure of certain provinces to reach an agreement was the reason for the lack of any such plan.
In dealing with this matter of a health plan I liken the minister to an old-time practitioner who has been called in to treat a patient. After he has treated him for some time the family become anxious, because he
Supply-National Health and Welfare does not admit that the disease is new to him. So he says, "Well, just keep on giving him doses of my special soothing syrup at regular intervals, and some time within the next three or four years I may find a cure." It is part of the policy of this party to initiate a health plan for the people of this country. It is all very well to keep stating that a health plan is part of the policy of this government, but I point out to the minister that the very things we hope to eliminate by the introduction of such a plan are in existence at the present time. There is no holiday, Mr. Chairman, from misery and suffering.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have all listened with keen interest, as we always do, to the remarks of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair). He always brings to the debate, on health matters particularly, the experience he has gained as a medical doctor and also a very obvious interest in the welfare of our people.
We are glad to note that the estimates of the department for this year, which are now before us, are up by some $19,402,227 to a new high of $396,348,311. I suppose some will say it is an old cry on the part of some of us, but I still think it is basically true that if this amount of money indicates the proportion of our national wealth that we are prepared to spend on the work of this department, we have not yet become sufficiently health and welfare conscious in this country. I realize that this is not the grand total. In fact I read with interest some weeks ago the report of a speech by the minister in New York, I believe, in which he made the statement that we were now spending in Canada close to a billion dollars a year on health and welfare. I was interested in where he got that figure, in view of the fact that the total for his department is less than $400 million; but on more closely reading the report of his speech I gathered that he had in mind the amounts spent at all levels of government, and perhaps amounts spent privately as well.
Basically the problem in connection with health and welfare is a financial one, to put it in the terms we understand most readily; but the problem is even more basic than that. The fundamental question is, do we value the health and security of our 13 million Canadian people sufficiently to plan the use of all our resources so that a sufficient portion will be set aside to take care of all our needs in the field of health and welfare. The present minister should, and I hope he will, do his share of fighting within the cabinet of which he is a member for an ever larger proportion of the national income for this purpose. If before I am through I say some things that are a bit critical, I hope he will realize that
2630	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Health and Welfare we on this side of the house are trying to be helpful, and that we are backing him up in his claim that more of the wealth produced in this country should be diverted to improving the health and security of our people.
In connection with the whole question of health, we welcome every little step forward. I am sure that the minister will recall the enthusiasm with which this group greeted the announcement of the Prime Minister in May, 1948, even though we knew at the time it failed to go as far as had been indicated in the previous pronouncements of the party. Nevertheless, I feel that I must say again that, in our view, the steps that have been taken with regard to health are just a beginning. In fact, they must be criticized as woefully inadequate.
As I see it, there are three things that the people of our country need before we can say that we are diverting a sufficient proportion of the wealth we produce to the care of our health. First of all, there must be the necessary personnel and equipment. There must be the doctors, nurses, dentists, technicians and all the people who work in the health field. Along with those people, there must be a sufficiency of hospitals, clinics and laboratories, to which patients may go and in which research work may be undertaken. Until we have a sufficient supply of personnel and equipment to take care of the health needs of our people, there is no room for the boasting that has been so aptly characterized by the member for Lanark (Mr. Blair).
As I see it, in addition to having doctors, hospitals and facilities, there must be ways and means to enable our people to get the medical services they require. In other words, it is no use having the best trained doctors or the best equipped hospitals, if our people cannot afford to go to them. That means we must make some real strides in the field of health insurance. I shall not go into too much detail on that subject at this moment, because there is an item for health insurance studies, and when we reach it I should like to ask the minister some questions. I am afraid they are the same questions that have been asked from this corner for many years. I hope, however, we shall receive more satisfactory answers this year than we have had in the past.
The whole point of health insurance is to make it possible for our people to be in a position where they can afford the services that should be provided. The idea of health insurance is to spread the costs around. No one in this chamber tonight, and the same is true of any collection of people of this number, knows which of us will need hospital or medical care within the next few months

or next year. It is a certainty that a percentage of us will need it. It so often happens that the need hits those who can least afford to pay for it, and vice versa. Surely, it is the civilized, common-sense thing to do, to plan the provision of medical and hospital care on some over-all basis, so that we shall be able to avail ourselves of those services.
I feel that both of those requisites I have discussed so far, the provision of personnel and equipment, and health insurance to enable our people to pay for the services that should be available, are of extreme importance. I am not satisfied, and I think that is the view of all Canadians, not just the view of a person in political opposition, with the pace of the progress we are making. The member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) has had something to say about hospital construction, and the shortcomings there are in that phase of the matter. I have already indicated that the answers we have received in the past with respect to health insurance suggest that progress in that field is particularly slow.
In addition to having personnel and equipment, and having health insurance to enable our people to pay for medical and hospital services, it is also the case that a large section of our people need to have sickness benefits. By "sickness benefits" I do not mean merely insurance to enable the people to pay hospital and doctor's bills, but a benefit to take the place of the pay envelope which so often stops in time of illness. I know that there are people in our country, no doubt some of them in this chamber, to whom this whole idea of the community concerning itself in the health and welfare of all, this whole idea of social security, is somewhat repugnant. The plain fact of the matter is that in our modern, highly complex industrial economy, no man liveth unto himself; no one is able to provide for all the things that can happen to him beyond his own control. It has become true that we stand or fall together. The sooner we move forward along the line of these common-sense ideas in the field of health, which I have tried to outline, the better it will be for all concerned, and for the nation as a whole. I feel very strongly that that is the position that should be taken by this government in the field of health; that we should get all we can in the field of personnel and equipment, that we should get health insurance on the statute books of this country without delay, and that there should be sickness benefits for our people in time of illness.
When I mention the latter subject, it does go further. It calls for an over-all social security program, towards which we must move as rapidly as we can. For the moment,

Supply-National Health and Welfare
I was trying to relate it particularly to the whole question of health. As I have indicated, however, this whole question does go over into the field of social security which falls within the jurisdiction of the same minister. Once more, I feel that it is not just a matter of something someone says because he is in political opposition, but it is a plain statement of fact that our people are not satisfied with the snail's progress that is being made in the field of social security, particularly with respect to old age pensions. In that connection, Mr. Chairman, while the question of old age pensions is a many-sided one, including such aspects as the amount of the pension, the age of the recipient and the means test, I should like to concentrate a few moments of my time tonight on the means test. It seems to me that there is no excuse for going any further in the life of this parliament without that old age pension means test being removed. Oh, I know there was a time when it was thought to be a perfectly proper part of the old age pension legislation. But that day disappeared at least five or six years ago. As the hon. member for Lanark has said, we have reached the point where all political parties in this house advocate the removal of the means test from the old age pension. Not only is it the case that all political parties advocate it, but from my contacts with people back in the constituency and in the city from which I come, and from the number of letters that I am receiving on the subject, I am convinced that the means test is now the most obnoxious feature of the old age pension as it stands.

What I was saying, Mr. Chairman, was that in the remarks I want to make now with respect to old age pensions I am concentrating on one phase of the subject. I feel that the amount should be higher. I feel that the age limit should be brought down. But at the moment I think that, to our Canadian people, the most obnoxious feature of the Old Age Pensions Act is the means test. You will remember that at that time the amount of the pension was increased, and that move was most acceptable; but the ceiling on the total income that pensioners could have was left where it was. That had the effect of actually reducing the amount of other income that pensioners can have before their pensions are reduced.
For example, it used to be that a single person could have $20 a month other income before his pension was reduced. Now a single person can have only $10 a month other income before his pension is cut down. It used to be that a married couple could have $30 a month between them by way of other income before they suffered a reduction in the amount of their pension. Now a married couple can have only $10 a month other income, or $5 each, before the amount of their pension is reduced. I think the minister will have to face the fact that it is largely because that amount of other income was narrowed as it was that people have become more incensed than ever over the means test. The fact is that a great many more persons than formerly now feel the effect of the means test and it comes fairly hard.
In addition to that, the cost of living has continued to rise and our older people have found it even more difficult to live as the months have come and gone. They are now finding that it costs them more to rent quarters in which to live, and all of these things have added to the burden on our old people. While, with thousands of them, the real issue is a larger pension, still it is also true that with a great many thousands the means test is the issue, and it is the feature that seems so particularly mean. Even if they are suffering as a result of it, people try to understand the government's not being able to raise the pension to a higher amount. But they simply cannot understand the meanness of the means test which places a penalty on people for such
[The Chairman.]

thrift as they have been able to exercise. In addition to that, there has been brought to our attention in recent months the collective bargaining for pension rights that has gone on particularly in the United States where some firms have granted pensions to their employees as part of what they are working for. But in those cases the pension is related to the old age pension or the social security benefit provided in the United States. For example, some of the companies there have now provided that their employees will get, when they retire, a total pension of $100 a month. But it is understood that that pension is made up of what they get from their government social security plus an amount from the company to bring it up to $100 a month. Trade union workers in this country know that there is no point in their trying to get that kind of an arrangement here because if they did get a decent pension out of their employers, the means test would prevent them from getting the old age pension on top of it.

In hundreds of cases their pensions are just enough to keep them from getting the old age pension. They see that other people who did not contribute to a pension plan are able, because they have nothing, to get the old age pension. These people who are receiving the pension to which they have contributed do not object to the other fellow, who needs it, getting it- not by a long shot. But they do feel that, since they have helped to build up the wealth of this country, and have paid taxes and the like, they should have the same privilege.
I urge upon the minister therefore that this is an extremely important issue which must be settled without further delay. During the election campaign of last May and June, to which reference is often made when debate in the house gets a bit warm, a great many members said they would fight for the elimination of the means test. I heard many Liberal candidates in my province say that that was one of the things they wanted to fight for-that the means test must go.
I have here an advertisement which appeared in the Vancouver News-Herald of June 13, 1949, advertising the candidacy of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. It says:
I will fight for a contributory retirement pension plan for all persons over sixty-five as a right. Pending the establishment of the foregoing act, I will fight for old age pensions to be paid to men of sixty-five and women of sixty without a means test, the pension to be large enough to ensure an adequate standard of living.
That is typical of the sort of thing that private Liberal candidates said throughout the country. What have they done about it since they came here? I want to be fair and say that you could not find a clear-cut promise like that in the official advertisements of the Liberal party which came from head office. The official advertising talked of what the party had done in the past. But 45781-168

My hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party made the same sort of statements, and so did Social Credit candidates. Certainly it has been our position in the C.C.F. for a long time. I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare in replying to this will not simply say, as he has said so often and so nicely in the past, that this still remains one of the objectives of government policy. We have had answers something like that ever since the failure of the dominion-provincial conference of 1945-46. The minister knows that one of the green book proposals at that time was that old age pensions should be raised from what they then were to $30 a month, and that it should be paid to all Canadians seventy years of age and over, without the means test. In addition to that it was to be paid 100 per cent by the federal government.
I suppose one can give a little credit to the federal government and say that they are now paying $30 of the $40 pension to those who are drawing it in full. But by Keeping the means test on many people do not get it in full. And it must be remembered that the cost of living has gone up a great deal since that proposal was made in August of 1945. That was a very commendable proposal; it brought hope to the hearts of many people. I would remind hon. members of the time it was made-two months after an election. The election was in June 1945, and in August, with the next election four years away, the government made the very interesting and worth-while proposal that the old age pension, so far as those seventy years of age and over were concerned, should be paid 100 per cent by the federal government, and without the means test.
We have reminded the minister of that proposal every chance we have had since that time; but the best we have been able to get from the minister, with his big broad smile, is that it still remains an objective of government policy. Well, let us not have any more of that this time. Let us not be told again that this cnange hinges upon a dominion-provincial conference and negotiations.
I am afrai:l that if we are not able, by hammering away, to get something done at this session or the next session, and if the government can get away without doing it

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in looking over these estimates for the Department of National Health and Welfare it is obvious that provision has been made for almost everything except some allowance for incurables. I would remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare of the extreme necessity for some system of allowances for those unfortunate people who have lost their earning power through accident, through injury or through some incurable disease. Provision has been made to some extent for old age pensions and for family allowances. Grants are to be made to the Canadian Welfare Council, the Health League of Canada, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind, the Victorian Order of Nurses and several others which I shall not mention. These are all worthy causes that are entitled to grants, but I suggest that the cause of the incurables is just as worthy of consideration.
Many of these people are not entirely helpless and with a little assistance they could do much toward earning their own living. I have here the Montreal Standard of November 19, 1949, which has an article dealing with leathercraft for tubercular patients. It gives the details of one patient who has been taught to manufacture handbags, wallets, belts and other articles and is thus able to earn his own living. There is no reason why we should not give assistance to these people in that way. Alberta has taken the lead in providing training for the victims of poliomyelitis, but we should go further than that.

This is more than a provincial matter. The unfortunate victims of these diseases and accidents are Canadian citizens and it is the duty of the federal government to provide means whereby they can be rehabilitated to earn their own living, or to provide allowances so that they will not have to depend on others for assistance. I urge the government to bring in a plan whereby these unfortunate people can be cared for.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with close attention to the hon. member for Lanark who told us that the minister had his finger pretty well on the pulse of the people, and for a few minutes I should like to outline to the minister what I consider is in the minds of the people at the present time. I intend to devote myself entirely to the question of pensions and I assure you that I shall not speak again when the item covering pensions is being considered.
I want the minister to know that at least in my opinion the question of security pensions has become one of immediate importance on the domestic scene. Workers in this country are daily becoming more security-minded. They are thinking in terms of pensions, health insurance and retirement plans. I feel sure that they are prepared to let the state assume a greater responsibility for their lives, whatever risk that entails; I feel that the risk is negligible. I submit that the wider your social security, the more secure is your democracy.
In connection with old age pensions the people are particularly disturbed about the means test. They feel that under present circumstances the means test makes the old age pension a handout. It requires the recipient to acknowledge his poverty and is a throwback to the poor laws of the' last century. One writer has described it as penalizing thrift, invading privacy, and socially objectionable. I believe the vast majority of the Canadian people are unalterably opposed to the means test, and I share that view with them. I take this opportunity to reiterate my opposition to it, an opposition which stems from my very inception into public life.
The people are interested not only in individual security; they are interested in collective security. There is a feeling which I share that industry has an obligation to take care of the depreciation of the human machine in the same way that it makes provision for the depreciation of the plant machine. United States industry has already committed itself to industrial and private pensions. Making due allowance for a time

Supply-National Health and Welfare
lag, the workers in this country are now entitled to and must get the same sort of security pension.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: And are getting it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They are not getting it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
