I should like to point out to the committee some of the statements that have been made by people who deal with pensions. According to the Toronto Star of September 30, 1949, George Burt, top man of the United Automobile Workers of Canada, said:
Pensions are the number one issue on our program this year.
Then Pat Conroy, referring to pensions, said:
This is a good start in laying the foundation for adequate social security for our workers. We have advised all our unions to include pension plans in their program this year.
Then George Burt made a further statement on September 14 that they were determined they would not accept anything less than the results of the negotiations in the United States.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is not a government pension.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am leading up to that. I point out that it will be impossible to refuse a pension to a Ford worker in Windsor when a Ford worker in Detroit receives it. It will be impossible to refuse a pension to a General Motors worker in Oshawa, when a General Motors worker in Pontiac receives it. They are both doing the same work, under the same conditions, for the same company.
I am aware that our pension problem is constitutionally involved, and that is one reason why I am speaking out tonight. A dominion-provincial conference is to be held some time in January. Not only must matters of jurisdiction and constitution be studied and discussed, they must be resolved. Unless we are able by the next session of parliament to give guidance and leadership in the matter of pensions we shall leave ourselves open to piecemeal, hodgepodge, unsatisfactory systems which will cover this country like a crazy quilt. I point this out to the minister. Pensions in Canada today lack uniformity. In the future if they are hammered out by collective bargaining they will in some Instances lack stability. They will have the
tendency to create problems for us rather than solve them. In the end they may not even give the security that they set out to give. What I am saying to the government tonight is that they must give leadership in the pension field. The government must set the pattern for a basic adequate pension. I know it is a great responsibility, and it calls for leadership now.
It may be that some people in the country think that we have gone too fast and too far already with social security. I do not share that view, and I do not think there are many who think that we should not now have a contributory form of old age pension. I am not one of those who are particularly disturbed by what happened in New Zealand a few days ago. What is good will remain, and it is hard at this distance to diagnose exactly what did happen. Nor was I disturbed when South Africa changed governments and took on a fascist tinge. I am more impressed by, and I think I shall learn more lessons from, the referendum on old age pensions that took place in the state of California, and the direct vote on the welfare state which took place in the state of New York. Both of these are much closer to the thinking of our people. As to contributory old age pensions, private and industrial pensions and health insurance, we have not gone far enough nor have we gone fast enough. Certainly there is need for integrating and co-ordinating the various systems that now exist, and which must be augmented by contributory old age pensions. It is true I have always been a partisan with respect to social security. Nevertheless I emphasize and want to impress again upon the government the importance of deciding on an all-embracing social security program which will give broad leadership in the confused problem of pensions. If we do not give leadership, if we continue to bicker over constitutional rights, the workers will take the solving of the problem upon themselves, and will hammer out the very best deal they can make.
Every member of the house realizes that industrial pensions have burst suddenly upon the United States scene. We have got a little time, and we can use it by doing some hard and fruitful thinking. Are we to have a contributory old age pension immediately? Are we to have industrial pensions, at least where companies are subsidiaries of United States companies, on the same basis as they have them in the United States? If industrial pensions are to be supplemented pensions, as they are in the United States, then I ask: supplementary to what and at what age? We must realize that we really have not got a

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak tonight on old age pensions, and I only do so for a moment because I have another subject I wish to discuss with the minister. I point out to myself and to others some difficulties that must be in the government's way in bringing in an over-all plan covering contributory old age pensions for everybody without a means test. I know that actuaries can give an answer having regard to certain schemes which are in vogue in many industrial companies, and which are growing daily. The hon. member for Spadina referred to Detroit and Windsor, and as we know there is a controlled subsidiary carrying on in Windsor in the province of Ontario. We know that history proves that what is adopted in one place so far as industrial relations are concerned is surely adopted in the other, and today they are on practically an even basis in the matter of employee treatment.
I am not big enough or smart enough to tell the minister how to treat outstanding pensions in our railways, banks and industrial companies. The hon. member for Spadina will recall that the concession at Detroit was only made a very short time ago. In other words, he is also aware that, so far as labour is concerned, the question of remuneration has changed largely from one of wages to one of security. One need only take that great union, the United Mine Workers of America, which was perhaps in the forefront of the new labour effort. I am not deriding it at all. If one believes in collective bargaining one must believe that strong unions are entitled to bargain, and if they do not get assistance from governments they must use the only weapons they have. When I hear somebody


has gone on strike I am not one of those people who immediately condemn them. I know they are using perhaps their only and certainly their best weapon to get what they think is their fair share from the earned industrial dollar. Together with the hon. member for Spadina I am and have for some time been in favour of a contributory pension which will look after not only organized labour but all our people, and particularly the white-collar workers who have no one to speak for them in this country because they are not organized.
You know, when John L. Lewis proposes something it is very easy to say, "Oh, that man again". Perhaps we use language a little more lurid than that; but if we are to be fair we must remember the condition of the miner in the United States and Canada before John L. Lewis rose to the top of that organization. To the shame of everyone, employer and public at large, those miners existed in a state which was disgraceful. Everything they got was obtained from the company store; they paid such prices as the company cared to charge; and until very recent years they lived in what were called company houses. I dislike lurid language, but they were practically wage slaves of the employers. Lewis now has a big head and thinks he runs the world, but I cannot help remembering the great advance in the comfort and incomes of the people who followed him.
I have already said I had no intention of speaking on the matter of pensions, but I do want to deal with one other subject, not in any super-critical fashion but in the hope that when the minister takes part in this debate he will deal with it at some length. I refer to the disease known as arthritis, on which I have had something to say every year since coming here in 1945. It may be that what I say tonight will be repetitive, though I hope not.
You can look at this matter in two harsh ways, if you like. The first is from the point of view of the time lost to the nation by people suffering from this illness. The figure given by the minister last session was 600,000 people suffering from that disease; I do not mean crippled, but suffering to the extent that they are unable to carry on their duties normally and earn a living, irrespective of the field of endeavour in which they were engaged. I assume that figure has increased since it was mentioned early last spring; but since that time I have had an experience which, if I were to consult only my own feelings, I should say I wish I had never undergone. Having interested myself in this matter I went to the town of Banff, where I

went through a hospital. It was not a large institution; I would not think there were more than seventy to one hundred people in the whole place.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That would be Dr. Robinson's hospital?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Dr. Robinson and his two sons are operating that hospital, and the father was good enough to take me through. I might add that this was after tfie election in June. There I saw things that would wring the heart of anyone. I am not going to mention many of them, but I wonder how many hon. members have gone through an institution like that. You are introduced to a patient who may be in bed or sitting up or perhaps even walking. The first thing that would occur to any of us, having been introduced, would be to shake hands; but when I put out my hand to a dear old lady I found she could not shake hands with me. All she could do was put her fist in my hand. Both hands were so tightly closed with this terrible disease that they were simply fists, and of course immediately I saw the swelling in the knuckles and joints.
I will admit that I was rather taken aback. I had been talking about this illness in the House of Commons. I knew the odd friend who was suffering from it, and had sustained a considerable dose of it myself. Then I went on and Dr. Robinson took me to a verandah, where I saw a little girl six years of age with the most beautiful face I have ever seen. I do not think I am exaggerating in that statement, because we all know that suffering often creates beauty, particularly in children. There she was with both legs and both arms utterly useless, with no development whatever. That child was in a condition from which, of course, she could never recover, so great was the hold the disease had taken upon her.
Then I saw a boy, to whom I spoke for quite a while. He was seventeen years of age, and looked fine. He shook hands with me and seemed quite happy. I said to Dr. Robinson, "I thought these were all arthritics." He replied, "Just a moment," and pulled down the blanket. Then he said, "Look at that knee." That seventeen-year old boy had a knee as big as a child's soccer ball. By that time I was pretty well sunk; but the doctor said, "Would you feel it?" I thought that I was being a little forward, but the lad laughed and said, "I don't mind, Mr. Smith," so I took my fingers, as I had seen the doctor do, and rapped that knee as I am rapping the desk now. It was solid bone. That boy of seventeen years was crippled for life; there was nothing they could do with that leg
Supply-National Health and Welfare except cut it off. There just was not and is not anything known to science which would be of any help to that young fellow.
Then I talked with the three doctors there. Since then I have talked with others, including my good friend from Lanark. As I understand it, the medical view is that we have advanced to the point where much can be done by way of special exercises and that sort of thing for people suffering from this disease but not completely crippled by it. But-and I make this statement with some timidity-as yet there is nothing known in the world about the cause. I know there is a kind which is not unusual; that is the traumatic type. Some of you who have played football may have a knee or some other joint which was injured, and an arthritic condition may immediately result. But as far as my inquiries have gone there just is not anything known about the origin of the rheumatoid kind, particularly where the disease is muscular. It appears to resemble rheumatism; that is where the phrase "rheumatoid arthritis" came from; but as yet we have found out practically nothing about it.
I am happy to learn that at an institution which I visited a little over a year ago some fine men have developed something which is called cortisone. It is developed in such minute quantities that it is not available as yet for the ordinary person, although I was happy to see in the newspaper the other day that these people were good enough to give Canadian research people some of it. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I believe our Canadian research people received a small portion of this drug in order that they might do some work on it. I believe it is derived from a gland in hogs, but you have to kill more hogs than can be killed in Chicago to get enough of this thing. The world is now searching, therefore, for something from which this drug might be produced synthetically.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit an interruption? This is an important matter, and I do not think I am over-exaggerating when I say that. I remember on one occasion I made a statement in this house, as a result of which many letters were received from many people who were suffering from this illness. As a result of that I thought that thereafter, whatever I would say about it, would be said only after the most careful consideration. There may be some people in this country who will form a judgment, from the last remark of the hon. member, that would not be justified under all the circumstances.
I know he shares with me the desire to refrain from stating any more than the actual situation. I am not criticizing, but I felt if I did

Supply-National Health and Welfare not say something now these remarks would be misconstrued and raise false hopes, at a time when I think the situation requires clarification. I propose to do that at the first opportunity.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I appreciate the interjection of the hon. minister, and I shall now try to see to it that nothing in my remarks will raise those false hopes.
I was just about to say that this drug is, in no sense as yet, a cure. The most that one can say about it is that it does give temporary relief. I believe that is what the minister had in mind. I believe a great deal more work has to be done upon it. It cannot be regarded as a cure, or even a palliative for general use.
I believe, Mr. Minister, I have gone as far as anyone can go in endeavouring to protect you from what you might have feared.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I think your statement is extremely helpful.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

Thank you. I mention that to show that successful work is being done, and I hope that some day there will be a corrective medicine for arthritics which will be what insulin has become for the diabetic. We well remember that insulin was not produced in a moment. It was produced after great study and research by Canadians working in the university of Toronto laboratories.
I turn now to this: Surely, there must be some way we can find the cause. It is not good enough to say that if you get this disease we can relieve those pains. I know a little bit about arthritic pain. The hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Robinson), if he were here and could rise on that arthritic knee of his, would agree with everything I have said up to the moment. I hope that when the minister takes up this subject he will devote some time to telling us what we in Canada are doing, not only in attempting to relieve a condition that is not permanent, but with respect to finding the cause. Mr. Chairman, the minister has nodded his head to indicate he is going to speak, so I shall conclude my remarks.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman. While I had intended to make a statement with regard to these matters at a later time, in view of the importance of this matter mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) I believe I should make that statement now so that his remarks will be associated with mine, having in mind the danger I mentioned a moment ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Can I say anything more? I shall do so if you desire.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No; what the hon. gentleman said was very helpful. There is a tremendous amount of interest, not only in this country, but all over the world, in the discovery of cortisone. As my hon. friend will see, we in the department have shared that interest in this problem with the people, and with the medical profession generally.
During the past year, medical research scientists have discovered that two new dirugs, ACTH and cortisone, seem to have extremely valuable results in the treatment of a number of diseases. It should be emphasized that the work that has been carried on now for some months is still in the experimental stage, and no final decisions have yet been reached on the full effects of these drugs, or of the illnesses and diseases for which they can effectively be used.
In April of this year, Dr. Philip Hench of Mayo clinic gave a public demonstration to medical scientists of the effects of the use of cortisone on arthritic patients. The results were almost miraculous, and because of this the drug cortisone has been associated popularly with arthritis. It should be emphasized, however, that this drug has not yet proved itself even for this single disease. It should also be emphasized that it seems to show promise for other diseases also.
I may say that I have had the advantage of personally talking-with Dr. Cameron, my deputy minister on the health side-with Dr. Hench and Dr. Kendall, both of whom must share the glory of what is undoubtedly a discovery of the first importance. It was shortly afterwards-after this research carried on by these two men-that the announcement was made about the drug ACTH, which seems to show similar promise, not only for arthritis but for other diseases. I must point out, and I say this with great emphasis, that both Dr. Kendall and Dr. Hench asked me whenever we made our statement-they asked the surgeon-general of the United States when he made his statement and the Merck Company, who will have something to do with it-to indicate that both ACTH and cortisone are in extremely short supply. At the present time the quantities available are not even sufficient for experimental purposes. There is no immediate prospect that the quantities that can be produced will exceed the needs of research workers, who are finding out the full effects of these drugs and subjecting them to prolonged tests. Both compounds are extremely difficult to produce. It has taken many years for research chemists to discover the various stages essential for their preparation. For example, the synthesis of cortisone requires several months

and thirty-seven individual stages of preparation that can only be carried out by highly skilled steroid chemists.
The history of ACTH goes back to the early 1920's when Dr. P. E. Smith in the United States discovered the influence of the anterior pituitary gland on the adrenal cortex. In 1933 a Canadian scientist, Dr. J. B. Collip, now dean of the medical school at the university of Western Ontario, prepared a comparatively pure extract from anterior pituitaries which was capable of replacing the pituitary gland in its power of influencing the adrenal cortex. Among many other scientists active in the development of ACTH, another Canadian, Dr. C. N. H. Long, formerly of McGill university, worked with Sayers and White at Yale university in obtaining purified ACTH from sheep and swine anterior pituitary glands. This discovery was simultaneous with that made by Li and Evans at the university of California. In 1948, Dr. C. H. Li and Dr. H. M. Evans worked out an analysis of ACTH to show that it possibly could be produced synthetically.
ACTH can be produced from the pituitary glands of sheep, cattle and swine. Swine glands have been shown to be the most productive. Other sources are under investigation.
Preparations are now actively going forward in the Department of National Health and Welfare, in the food and drug division, to set up acceptable assay standards to check the potency of ACTH produced in Canada or imported into Canada.
The story of cortisone is similar to that of ACTH. It was in 1925 that Drs. Rogoff and Stewart of Harvard university showed that an extract of the adrenal cortex of animals would prolong the survival time of animals that had had their adrenal glands removed. In 1930 Hartman, formerly of the university of Toronto, and Brownell; and Swingle and Pfiffner independently discovered a method of extraction of the adrenal compound cortin which served as the basis for commercial production.
Because of what is undoubtedly going to be a matter of the greatest importance, in making this statement I wanted to put on record the participation of some of our own Canadian medical scientists. In 1934, the Connaught Laboratories of Toronto was one of the three laboratories that pioneered in the production of cortin which is used in the treatment of Addison's disease.
The story of the development of cortisone is long and involved. This can be understood when it is realized that cortisone is simply one out of twenty-eight different compounds that have been isolated from the adrenal
Supply-National Health and Welfare cortex. Among the many scientists in the United States and Canada who contributed to the development of cortisone, the name of Dr. E. C. Kendall of the Mayo clinic is perhaps best known. I would want to say at once to him and to Dr. Hench that I am quite sure I speak for the Canadian people when I say that we have learned of the development of this story with the greatest interest, and our gratitude to them will of course know no bounds. We appreciate the great collaboration, the promise and the actual help that has been given in making certain guarantees that production, if and when that takes place, will be available to Canada.
Among Canadians who have made important contributions to the development of cortisone are Dr. R. D. H. Heard and Dr. J. S. L. Browne, both of McGill university; and also Dr. Hans Selye of the university of Montreal. The contribution made by these Canadian scientists to the development of cortisone is similar to that made in the development of ACTH by Dr. J. B. Collip, now head of the medical school at the university of Western Ontario, and Dr. James Campbell of the university of Toronto. Dr. L. I. Pugsley, chief of the food and drug laboratory in our own department, was coworker with Dr. Collip when he prepared a substance which was one of the steps towards the development of ACTH.
In the food and drug laboratory of the Department of National Health and Welfare, in addition to Dr. Pugsley there is Mr. W. D. Snair, who took his M.Sc. degree with Dr. James Campbell of the university of Toronto whom I have just mentioned. As a result, this department is now going forward actively with plans to establish assay techniques to check both cortisone and ACTH. There are a number of sources for cortisone, some well established, others in the experimental stage.
Now I simply want to say one or two further things in connection with this matter. On Monday last, Merck and Company Limited, with head offices in this country and in the United States, announced at Rahway, New Jersey, that it believes increased production of cortisone will enable it to supply various teaching medical centres with limited quantities for research purposes. The company has noted that cortisone shows promise of relief of certain types of arthritis, acute rheumatic fever and certain other diseases and that the compound will be available after January 1. I must clearly indicate the position, because already requests quite naturally are coming in from all over the country asking for some of this cortisone.

Supply-National Health and Welfare I can say nothing about the future, but at the present time what quantity will be available to us-and it will be made available to us after January 1

will be solely for experimental research purposes. But every effort that we know how to make is going to be made to see if there cannot be acceleration of the process of production and of research into further uses. We have established contacts with a number of medical men who are expert in this field and who have had contacts with Dr. Kendall and Dr. Hench and the scientific committee that has been established in the United States. I want to give to hon. gentlemen and to this country the assurance that no effort is going to be spared to do all that can possibly be done through this department, more particularly through Canada's research scientists on whom the development really rests. No effort will be spared. I hope perhaps before the end of next week to say something further in that connection but at this stage I feel that I should await the result of certain conferences that are taking place elsewhere before I make that announcement.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will take up as the first item of business the amendments to Bill No. 12, ot establish the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation; then we will take up Bill No. 215, to amend the Dominion-Provincial Tax Rental Agreements Act, 1947; Bill No. 219, to amend the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; Bill No. 200, to amend the Customs Act. Then we will go into supply and call the estimates of the Department of Labour, reconstruction and supply, national revenue and mines and resources; and from eight to nine private bills.

I would suggest to the minister that there should not be a sitting tomorrow night. We have had a very heavy week, sitting eight hours each day. After all, we are here to do the business of the country, and it is a difficult matter for the parties in opposition to do their work properly if the house is going to sit on Saturday evening. We have to have some time to prepare for the work which will come up.
I do suggest the house should not sit tomorrow night. I believe if that sitting is dispensed with we shall make better progress next week. We are all just as anxious to get home as are the members of the government; but the situation is that it is simply impossible to carry on efficiently under this pressure, unless some time is given to prepare the work.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is inhuman.

May I add my voice to that of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, and ask the minister to adjourn at six o'clock tomorrow night. I do not think he will make any more progress by keeping us here for the evening; because we are being worn ragged here twelve hours a day-and we have other work to look after as well. If the minister insists upon keeping us here I am afraid that in the temper we shall be in he will not make much progress. I would suggest therefore that, for harmony all round, we be allowed to have the night off.

May I add my voice to the pleas which have been made to the house leader. I think that if we sit tomorrow until six o'clock we shall have done a pretty fair week's work; and I would ask that he be just a little sympathetic.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The government should make it unanimous.

The house leader might do this: There are the faithful fifty who spend every night here; why not get another shift from the crowd who are not here. Let them sit tomorrow night.
